speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the Government, and on the amendment of Mr. Johnston (Saint-Henri-West-mount), p. 5043, and on the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Riis (Kamloops-Shuswap), p. 5047.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question? The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am ready for my speech, not for questions.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was informed it was time to resume debate, but the Hon. Member is not in the House. Debate. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are one or two things to welcome in this Budget. As you know from the other day, I had proposed that the Government look favourably on the plight of home brewers who have been forced to act illegally for many years. This has been addressed in the Budget, but it is unfortunate that it is one of the very few things that was addressed in the Budget that affects ordinary Canadians. I want to speak about the impact of this Budget on ordinary Canadians, the impact of the Budget on people in the Province of Quebec, and about the way that the Budget is going to affect people in my riding of Ottawa Centre and people living in the National Capital Region.
Perhaps I can put on the record what the impact of the Budget will be on a family earning $30,000 or $40,000 a year, a middle-income family which has been trying to get by and finding it very difficult with the present cost of food, housing and the other essentials that it needs in order to survive. At the time of the November statement, the new Government effectively increased the tax burden on that average family by about some $500 per annum by incorporating the sales tax
increase which it had previously resisted in opposition when it had been proposed by the Liberal Government, and by bringing in other tax measures which had that effect.
It has done it again. The increase in the taxes on the average family in the new Budget will be of the order of $500 per family; $100 through the elimination of the federal tax reduction, $115 in loss to the average family through the modification of indexing; $22.50 through the cut in family allowance payments; some $75 of increase if that family smokes and drinks the occasional bottle of beer or wine; the sales tax increase will cost the family $150; and the gas tax, as a very conservative estimate, will cost $ 1 a week on a tank of gas, or another $50 a year. That adds up to $512.50 for the average family.
The promise of the Budget was that it would be tough but fair. It certainly is tough on that family who now has to pay $1,000 a year more in taxes than it had to pay just a year ago, thanks to the new Conservative Government. The toughness is reflected in the fact that by 1990, the Government expects that personal income taxes will rise by $4.1 billion and that sales and excise taxes will rise by another $2.6 billion. The fairness will be fair only to a very limited proportion of the tax-paying public.
Corporation taxes are expected to fall by $2.2 billion by 1990 according to budget figures. In other words, it is more taxes on individuals and less taxes on corporations. That unfairness is particularly evident if you look at what the Government has done with the $500,000 exemption for the capital gains tax. That will cost $300 million in 1985. It will result in $600 million in lost revenue in 1986. The Government does not estimate what it will cost in subsequent years, but since the limit on capital gains that will be tax free goes up year by year, one has to assume that we will be talking about $1 billion or more per annum, which is being given not to every Joe and Jane across the country, but is being given to that small proportion of the tax-paying public who have the disposable income and can benefit on substantial amounts of capital gains.
If the Government had said that it wanted to encourage small business and encourage people to launch themselves into equity investment by making a certain small proportion of capital gains tax free, I would not have been happy about it, but I could have at least seen the point. However, huge profits on Miami condominiums, the New York art market and the London Stock Exchange will all be eligible for this treatment. It does not make a lot of sense, particularly when you look at who is paying.
Who is paying? One of the major groups that is paying is old age pensioners. They will give up the equivalent of $225

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Cassidy
million in pension next year due to the de-indexing of the Old Age Security. That money is not being applied, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said over the weekend, to reduce the deficit. It is being applied to give a great, big fiscal carrot to the top 5 or 10 per cent of taxpayers who will get this capital gains tax elimination beginning next year. That is not fair in any kind of taxation system that I can understand.
During the election campaign, Progressive Conservative Members promised a minimum tax at the urging of NDP Members. Now they have deferred that minimum tax. At the same time, they have opened up the most glaring loophole yet for upper-income earners in the form of the $500,000 exemption.
Back in the 1960s when the Carter report came out, the concept which I thought was reasonable was that a buck is a buck is a buck. Certainly when one spends a dollar earned through capital gains, it has the same spending power as a dollar earned through an employment salary or income. However, that is not reflected in the Budget. After the Liberals eroded the tax base in the corporate sector, the Progressive Conservatives now intend to erode the tax base in the personal tax sector by taking tax burdens away from people who are upper-income earners.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the situation in the Province of Quebec, in connection with the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). This spring and during the winter, the New Democratic Party's Task Force on Unemployment travelled through Quebec. We went to Quebec City, Montreal, Chicoutimi and the Outaouais to meet people, union members and workers, community groups and municipalities, to talk about the priorities they were seeking in the Budget.
The situation in Quebec is not very good. The unemployment rate is still over 12 per cent, Mr. Speaker. There has been a slight drop since April 1984, but nevertheless, we still have a situation where one out of eight workers is unemployed. Among young people, the unemployment rate in many parts of Quebec is over 20 per cent. In Chicoutimi, for instance, it is as high as 26 per cent. Time and time again, Quebecers told us they were looking for positive action to boost the economy in their province, and they told us about some very important community projects they were ready to start with the support of their government, meaning not just the Government of Quebec but also the Government of Canada. Now I am well aware that Mr. Duhaime, the Quebec Minister of Finance, "welcomed" Mr. Wilson's Budget. These are two birds of a feather, Mr. Speaker. We have in Quebec a government that we could now call a Conservative PQ government, because they have the same views on budget priorities. However, Mr. Speaker, these priorities do not provide anything for the average Quebecer.
In Chicoutimi people are wondering what the Budget is going to do for them at a time when the forestry industry is not doing enough reforestation and the region's main industrial base, the aluminum industry, cannot provide new jobs. It is a desperate situation, but at the same time, we see people who are looking for projects and for the necessary funding and resources to help the economy in their own region get back into gear.
Mr. Speaker, what is the Budget doing for farmers in Quebec? The answer is: nothing! What is the Government doing for disadvantaged regions? The answer is: nothing! What has the Government done for farmers and the agricultural industry? There again, the answer is: nothing! I remember how during the election campaign, the Conservatives, or rather the Hon. Member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), wrote a symbolic cheque for pork producers, by giving them access to the Federal Stabilization Fund. Unfortunately, this promise was not kept. During the election campaign, the Conservatives promised an enormous sum of money to finance farm mortgages at reasonable rates: another promise that was not kept.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me this new Government is not listening, because it was very obvious on September 4 that Quebecers voted for a change of government at the federal level. They were fed to the teeth with the Liberals. They wanted to get rid of the Liberal Government and bring about real change that would benefit everyone in Quebec, and not just the businessmen on St. James Street: the Paul DesMarais, the Westmount bankers and the rich in Quebec generally. But what are this Government's priorities regarding Quebec? Of course, the deficit is their priority. I welcome their gesture to the solidarity fund, and I say it is a step in the right direction. But aside from that, they have done nothing that is going to have any effect on Quebec's disadvantaged regions.
Quebec is not just St. James. It is not just the Montreal area. Quebec is the Gaspe, Chicoutimi, Lac-Saint-Jean, the Abitibi area and the Eastern Townships, Mr. Speaker. Quebec is the Saint-Maurice area and Trois-Rivieres, and all these regions are suffering from a lack of jobs. Their basic industries are threatened, and nothing is being done by the Federal Government to help these industries and to help save the province's economic base.
Under the former PQ Government, I mean the Government that was in power before 1985, real efforts had been made to promote consultation between Quebec's various regions and its major industries. There were economic summits in each region, attended by employers, industries, municipalities, community groups, unions and workers. Everyone was involved in looking for ways to rebuild and boost their industries and regions. And in each case, Mr. Speaker, it was clear that federal assistance was needed, because the Federal Govern-
May 27, 1985

ment was just as involved in Quebec's economy as the Quebec Government.
Now, in order to implement the consultation policy proposed at these economic summits, it will just not do to maintain a policy of ignoring, of patently ignoring Quebec's needs. The Federal Government's participation is necessary to help specific industries and specific regions to get back on track. That is what is lacking in this Budget, Mr. Speaker. One wonders, for instance, how the capital gains exemption is going to help Quebec's shipyards, where the present situation is that 60 per cent of shipyard workers are out of work. The problem is that Davie Shipyards in Lauzon has just laid off half of its workforce, with the remaining half to be laid off this fall. The Government, however, continues to ignore the promise it made last August to give $75 million to the shipbuilding industry. In fact, it has had to withdraw the shipyard subsidy program, effective the end of June 1985.
That is the Government's policy on one of Quebec's major industries. As far as forestry is concerned, Mr. Speaker, no promises were made. And the same applies to the manufacturing industry in Quebec. Even in the Montreal area, the citizens' committee noted that the future of Petromont was not dealt with in the Budget; that today, with the reduction of subsidies to VIA Rail, the future of VIA Rail's maintenance centre is again in doubt; that privatization of Crown corporations as suggested in the budget is specially threatening to Montrealers, because many corporations are located in Montreal. The committee also noted that there was no reference to strategic proposals for Montreal's future as a transport and communication centre or international banking centre.
Mr. Speaker, we must have participation. We do not, however, need consultations between Mr. Duhaime and Mr. Wilson on measures that will compromise the future of the Province of Quebec. We must work together to provide a better economic base for Quebec, and that is what the New Democratic Party proposed through its employment task force. We must work together with all groups in the Province of Quebec, not just those that supported the Progressive Conservative Government's election campaign.

I would like to comment briefly on a number of areas in the Budget which have troubled me. However, there are one or two areas in the Budget which might have some promise.
In the area of pensions, the Government is promising two-year vesting, better provisions for women, and increasing portability. Those are good measures, except for the fact that they will not come into effect until after 1987 and, therefore, there will be no workable benefit until 1989 and no pension entitlement earned prior to 1987 will count. That is inadequate, Mr. Speaker, and makes this forward-looking promise effectively worthless as far as most Canadians are concerned.
The Budget-Mr. Cassidy
In the area of research and development, the Government makes bold promises, but the Minister of Finance ignored in his speech the fact that just last week the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) effectively repudiated the Government's campaign promise to double Canada's percentage of research and development spending to 2.5 per cent by 1990.
While the measures in the Budget may be welcome to small companies, they will come nowhere near to undoing the damage that has been done by the Government's destruction of federal public research and development efforts, its undermining of the National Research Council, and the fact that the Government has not been prepared to bring forward a plan to see how we increase the 1.3 per cent of spending on research and development to the proposed 2.5 per cent.
I would like to talk briefly about a situation right here in Ottawa in my home riding. Ottawa is a bit of a microcosm of the country in how it is affected by the Budget. We are fortunate that our unemployment rate is down around 8.5 per cent. That is better than that in the country as a whole. But with the cut in 15,000 government jobs over the course of the next six years, there will be no job opportunities for the young people coming out of high school, community colleges and universities here in Ottawa. I repeat, there will be no job opportunities because of the loss of about 15,000 potential jobs which would have been created in Ottawa over the course of the next six years. That is almost equal to the total number of young men and women coming out of grade 12 in schools in Ottawa over the course of the next five or six years. There will be an awful lot of job opportunities which will dry up.
There may be some increased employment in the high-tech sector. I hope that that is in fact the case. Nonetheless, we have a lot of running to do in Ottawa just to catch up with the situation which was created by the government's cut-backs. In addition to that, one has to be aware of the fact that there is a very real danger that good jobs in Government will be replaced by part-time help, minimum wage and contracted out jobs because of the Government's policy of putting jobs into the private sector. There is a real prospect that essential services to Canadians will be no longer available by the cut-back of 15,000 jobs. I bring to the attention of the Government the fact that already in the Canada Employment and Immigration service, there have been cut-backs at a time when overtime has been used as a matter of course week after week and month after month by CEIC employees who are trying to provide services to unemployed Canadians. Even now they cannot keep up with the demands which are being made upon them.
As far as the young people in Ottawa are concerned, Mr. Speaker, the unemployment rate is running around 14 per cent or 15 per cent, and I note that the student employment centres at Carleton Unversity and other universities will be closed. The Government is effectively making life extremely difficult for those young people who really deserve more from Government. They deserve more from us in Parliament than they are getting in this particular Budget.

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Cassidy
I would also like to speak on behalf of the superannuated federal government employees and plead with the Government not to assume that it can simply, with the stroke of a pen, take away the indexing for which these pensioners have been paying in their pension contributions these past many years. The Budget of the Finance Minister seems to take it as assumed that it is OK to take away that indexing. I want to tell the Minister of Finance that there are a lot of superannuated federal public servants who are extremely concerned. People have called me in the last couple of days almost crying over the telephone because they don't know how they can survive if the indexing which enables them to cope with the cost of living is in fact not going to be maintained. The Budget ignores the fact that negotiations with the Public Service Alliance and other unions have not so far been successful. The Public Service employees have earned that indexing. If something else is put in its place, those employees have to be guaranteed that they are still being fairly dealt with. That is not being done right now, Mr. Speaker, and that worries me very much. I will continue, as one representative of the people of the Ottawa area, to make sure that they are not unfairly dealt with in this Budget.
I would like to ask the Government to assure the House that there will be no lay-offs of Public Service employees as a consequence of this Budget, because that would be a particularly cruel, unpleasant and undesirable result of the Budget.
I would like to conclude by saying that we in the New Democratic Party saw the prospect for a positive Budget rather than just eight months of rumbling before a mouse emerged from the Government. We foresaw a Budget which would be fair to ordinary Canadians rather than only to people who have the prospect of earning $.5 million in capital gains tax free. We thought that we could set unemployment reduction targets as they did in the Province of Manitoba to reduce unemployment by 2 per cent or 2.5 per cent this year. That would have been fair to ordinary Canadians.
We saw the prospect for investing in our future in areas such as the upgrading of resources, community development, technological development, housing, and municipal investments. We saw the prospect of bringing ordinary Canadians on board in terms of research and development by ensuring that they would be partners in technological change rather than victims of new technology. We saw the prospect of reforming the tax system to sweep away that $15 billion or $20 billion of tax concessions to corporations which contribute so much to the deficit and are creating such a difficult situation for Canadians.
Rather than that, Mr. Speaker, those concessions are essentially untouched and the surtax which has been put on upper income Canadians and corporations is for one year only, whereas the benefits to upper income Canadians and large corporations will go on in perpetuity. Mr. Speaker, this Budget is reminiscent of the Budgets of Ronald Reagan in the United
States. It is not quite as vicious or brutal on the surface, but the philosophy is the same. We have seen in the United States, in British Columbia, and in Great Britain that the approach of putting money in the pockets of the rich in hopes that it trickles down to the poor is not an effective policy for creating jobs for Canadians. That is why we have grave reservations about this Budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member knows that the Progressive Conservatives have led the way in demanding a minimum tax on the rich. We promised that minimum tax during the election and we brought it in in the Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Your nose is getting longer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am going to give the Hon. Member a chance. Let him just wait a moment.
We announced a minimum tax in the Budget effective January 1, 1986. We brought forward a discussion paper laying out three methods. As a chartered accountant I am tempted to ask the Hon. Member which method he prefers, but that would be unfair because at this point I, as a chartered accountant, am not exactly sure which method will do what we want it to do in terms of taxing the rich. That is not my question. We have provided for consultation with the people. We have provided for examination by a parliamentary committee. We have said that it will start on January 1. I suggest to the Hon. Member that that process is fair to the taxpayer and also to the tax collector. In my opinion, it would create undue chaos to introduce that type of tax in the middle of a fiscal year. I think the Hon. Member would agree that that type of tax must be instituted at the start of a taxation year.
Why are we not getting support from the NDP after we brought in this minimum tax? This lack of minimum tax has been nothing but a Liberal ploy to benefit their friends in big business. We brought it in. Why can we not get some support from the NDP for the process and the principle both of which are important? Will we have the support of the NDP when we go to committee in order to get the best result rather than the usual moaning and groaning?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the Government had brought in a minimum tax in this Budget, one which was tough and effective, he would have had the support of the NDP.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
By deferring in order to have consultation, the Government is going to give every advantage possible to the former colleagues of the Minister of Finance in Dominion Securities and to the financial interests in Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal to find ways of cutting down the minimum tax
May 27, 1985

to the point where it will be a piece of cosmetic window-dressing and nothing else.
Why did the Government not defer the de-indexing of old age pensions for a year until it has had a chance to consult with old age pensioners to discover whether they would be in favour of that? Why did the Government not defer the increase in the sales tax until it has had a chance to consult with ordinary Canadians to discover whether they were prepared to pay and thought it was a fair tax, particularly when the revenue is required mostly to pay for the concession of capital gains? The Government wasted no time putting the capital gains tax exemption into effect for the 1985 tax year in order to give something to the rich. However, in attempting to tax people who are very rich, the Government gave them every opportunity to resist it by a process of added consultation.
If the Government introduces a tough and effective minimum tax and makes it retroactive to 1985, it will have our support. However, I do not believe that is its intention.
I would also point out that the New Democrats have been talking about a fair tax system year after year. When the Hon. Member was in opposition, did he talk about a minimum tax? It was only when his leader was challenged by our leader in the television debate during the election campaign that the Conservatives finally committed themselves to some form of minimum tax.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre-where I reside three and a half days a week-and when I heard him talk about a microcosm I thought he ought to get out of it now and then, as suggested earlier by my colleague.
When New Democratic Party Members claim that they crisscrossed the country to consult Canadians-

speechtext:
Nor did they ever come anywhere near my place either because, had they done so and travelled throughout Quebec they would have found out that, barely a few weeks ago, the Minister of State (Forestry) (Mr. Merrithew) signed a $300 million agreement with the Province of Quebec. Three Ministers were there-two from Quebec, one from Ottawa- along with 15-odd Members representing various Quebec regions to witness this agreement to spur the forest industry which the previous Government ignored for years. Here they are now saying that we have not done anything for forestry. You could at least check your notes and those of your colleagues who were involved in the consultation process, if indeed they were.
The Hon. Member talked about shipyards, and I wondered whether we both read the same newspapers. Everybody knows that an agreement was signed recently to put Lauzon's Davie
The Budget-Mr. Cassidy
shipyards back in business at a time when the shipbuilding industry is in the doldrums not only in Quebec and the rest of Canada, but throughout the world as well. Of course, Marine Industries on the shore of the Richelieu River are in a predicament as a result of the on-going strike, and all parties involved are trying to arrive at a settlement which will serve the interests of the unions and those of the Quebec Government which happens to be an active partner. The federal Government has nothing to do with that. We have contracts and we are living up to our commitments with the shipbuilding industry as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, I wish the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) would tell us just what he thinks of those special measures taken even before the Budget was brought down. Consultations had been going on for years, but to no avail because the federal Government did not do anything. Well, in six months, we did consult, we sat down with the Minister and hammered out an agreement. Why should you say that the forest industry was left out in the Budget?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I note that my friend still talks as though Ottawa is not representative of the rest of the country, as if it were privileged territory. I can assure him that a lot of people who live here in Ottawa know something about substandard housing, are affected by unemployment, earn incomes below the national average and have to cope with the same problems as those experienced by his constituents.
I do not particularly fancy the remarks of his colleague the Parliamentary Secretary who has just suggested the new Government should ignore Ottawa because the city has been so generously treated in the past. Mr. Speaker, I too have constituents who must live with their problems. If we were to look at the situation of the shipbuilding industry, among others, I can tell my colleague that 60 per cent of the shipyards workers are idle. But in spite of that and the Prime Minister's promises in an August 26 speech before the Toronto Empire Club, as I recall, the Government has scrapped its $75 million assistance program for shipbuilders. The Lauzon shipyards were not spared despite the fact that, after the Government announcement, they laid off half their work force and will dismiss the other half this fall because there are no contracts. How can the Government remain so indifferent to the plight of that industry? I simply cannot understand.
Now, Mr. Speaker, concerning agriculture, the Government-

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this opportunity to participate in the budget debate allows me to put on the record the views of my constituents as well as the considerations from a social policy point of view that make this Budget worthy of support. I am pleased to have this opportunity.
No Member of the House-certainly no Member of the Government-takes any pleasure in the fact that there are those who say that the Budget is tough. However, we do take a measure of pride in the fact that we have attempted to be fair in the manner in which the Budget addresses Canada's economic crisis. My colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), has done an admirable job of seeking out a national consensus for the direction of the Budget by taking often divergent views and opinions and bringing about a fair and balanced Budget.
I said that Canada faced an economic crisis. I believe very strongly that such has been the case and that we will be on such a crisis footing for some time. This is a crisis not only in the economy but, as a result, in all aspects of our social and national life.
Let me illustrate by reminding the House that during the last years of aggravated conflict between Ottawa and the provinces, many of us argued that the failure of the federal Government to show national economic leadership increased the strain on Confederation. The weak state of the economy led to many of the inter-regional and federal-provincial conflicts that we witnessed during those years.
In the same way, failure to recognize an economic crisis as a crisis can only put in jeopardy the social security system and the social infrastructure that, as parliamentarians and Canadians, we cherish so much.
This Government recognized the gravity of the economic situation and we have acted. More to the point, the Government recognized what would be the inevitable consequences of our economic problems and we have acted now.
If Members of the House are honest with themselves, they will know that tough choices had to be made. We know, having been in the Opposition, how very easy it is to sit in the Opposition and decry hard choices, claiming that the pain was somehow avoidable. I can understand that posture, and in fact I hear some Members today using that very same argument.
However, being the Government is another story. To do nothing about the situation that was described to the House by the Minister of Finance last Thursday would be irresponsible and would have earned the scorn of the Canadian public. First and foremost, that situation to which I refer is the mounting public debt, flowing from a national deficit that has skyrocketed in the last two decades. Without action, the deficit this year would have been over $38 billion and next year over $40 billion. The debt is not a myth. Nor is the debt a fictitious monster or, for that matter, as some in the Opposition might want us to believe, is it a benign giant. The debt is a burden. It is a burden which is real, a burden which is heavy, and a burden which will affect decisions made both in the House and by Canadians as individuals. The debt will not go away by wishing it to do so. Without determination to arrest the debt, sooner or later it would lead to the paralysis of the Government of Canada. Being the Minister responsible for the Department which consumes roughly a quarter of the federal budget, I see first-hand on a day by day basis the costs of our social infrastructure, and I am inclined to believe that the paralysis would come sooner rather than later.
Let me put it into an even clearer perspective, from the point of view of the Department. At the present time the cost of the debt to Canadians is approximately $22 billion on an annual basis. The total cost of health care to the provinces and the federal Government is approximately $22 billion. Thus today we are spending as much to service the debt as Canadians across the country spend for health care. Anyone with a bit of understanding, regardless of his or her partisanship, will have to come to the quick conclusion that that loss of money, money which does not buy a new service, brings into jeopardy the very services we want to maintain. Or, to put it another way, the $22 billion of debt is roughly equal to federal government, federal taxpayer, expenditures for the federal share of health care costs and pensions combined. We as Canadians spend about the same amount on the debt today as we do on the federal share of health care and pensions.
If we could reduce the cost of that debt by 25 per cent, we as the federal Government, as federal taxpayers, would have 50 per cent more money for health care, or we would have 50 per cent more money than we are spending now on pensions, or a combination thereof, obviously. When people talk to me about the Budget not having a social policy component, I say they are wrong. The fact is that to retain social policy we have to create wealth and, if we do not have wealth or if we do not create wealth, we cannot have a sustained social policy. If Hon. Members opposite do not believe that, all they have to do is to take a look at some of their neighbours in the international community to make that point.
Being a Member from the Province of Manitoba, a province which is dependent to some degree on transfer payments, I realize that it is also important from that perspective to understand that debt costs are losses to those provinces and citizens as well.
I should like to make another argument. There are those who say that we should raise the deficit and create employment. I ask them a simple question. We now have a very high deficit. I have shown the cost of the debt. If that is the case, and if that system works, why do we still have 1.4 million Canadians unemployed? Surely, as Hon. Members return to

May 27, 1985
their ridings, as I did this weekend-and I had a number of meetings with senior citizens, business people, farmers-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did they think?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell the Hon. Member, because he loves to speak from the seat of his pants. What they were saying-and they were understanding it-was that we could not sustain those kinds of debt charges and still maintain the services they wanted to see maintained. Another point they made was that they were pleased as farmers and as small business people that pools of capital which they had earned would stay in their hands as a result of the capital gains changes. What will they do with that capital? They will invest it in their farms and on Main Street, Canada.
What I am saying to Hon. Members opposite, to everyone, is that when they look at job creation and at social policy, they should start relying on their neighbours and their vision of their communities. They should start relying on the ability of their friends and neighbours to invest in their communities so that they can create infrastructure and jobs for their children. They should start relying on their friends, not always think that Government will do better for communities than their friends and neighbours can do.
For too long, I believe, economic policy and social policy have been treated in isolation. I believe the Canadian public knows more than we in the House give them credit for knowing. Action was needed to restore fiscal integrity to our national affairs. Canadians are not prepared to see a greater and greater percentage of our finances devoted to carrying interest charges on the national debt when our social services and hospitals are choked for funds, yet that is exactly what was threatened. The public will not tolerate the continued reality of waste and efficiency in public expenditure at the expense of flexibility to meet new social needs or to seize new economic opportunities. In the vital challenge of creating new jobs, Canadians increasingly want priority placed on effective and permanent solutions, not short-term band-aids. These national objectives-security of our social programs, flexibility to meet new needs, and lasting solutions to the unemployment crisis-are addressed by the Budget.
The Budget involves certain adjustments-adjustments to promote private sector job creation, adjustments to reform employer-sponsored pension plans to assist Canadians in their retirement income planning, and adjustments to a new competitive economic environment in which the realities of markets make it easier to help workers adapt to new employment than to subsidize a failed industry. If we had not made those hard choices now, we would have had to make even harder choices down the road. In the face of that reality it would have been irresponsible-and I suggest to the House heartless-to put off the inevitable.
It would be inaccurate in the extreme to portray this Budget, as those in the Opposition have tried to do, as a bad news Budget. About 185,000 disabled persons, for example, will benefit from a new definition of disability for the purposes of the Income Tax Act. Many Canadians suffering from
The Budget-Mr. J. Epp
disabling conditions, who are presently neither blind nor confined to a bed or to a wheelchair, do not have access to this deduction from taxable income. The new definition to be administered by experts in the Department will improve the situation for these Canadians. In this action the Government has responded to the Special Parliamentary Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped by promoting the role of independent living.
Other speakers in this debate may well refer to the assistance to artists contained in the Budget. Tax changes affecting artists recognize their unique professional circumstances and seek to make it easier to donate works of art to public charities and to write off the costs of their inventories.
The voluntary community which forms part of the experience of every Member of the House will benefit from two changes to the treatment of their tax affairs. It will now be easier to donate gifts of intangible capital property to charities, and the Budget clarified the right of charitable organizations to engage in non-partisan political activity.
Members also know that while preserving the principle of universality, as we said we would do, the structure of the child benefits system has been made more progressive. The new structure provides a better basis for changes that any future Parliament may wish to make in response to the evolving needs and circumstances.
More than with any of these advances in social policy contained in the Budget, I am pleased by the reforms to the pension system announced by my colleague, the Minister of Finance. I take this opportunity to stress again that the Government is not closing the doors on pension reform with these announced changes to the Pension Benefits Standards Act. Rather, reforms to the Canada Pension Plan, including the proposal of a home-makers' pension, remain the firm commitment of the Government. The Minister of Finance has already had some discussions with the provinces in this area. We will each be pursuing this discussion with our provincial colleagues in the months to come.
In the meantime, these improvements to minimum pension standards for private pension plans under federal jurisdiction should be given recognition for what they are, that is, major improvements in the rules for vesting, portability and survival benefits. We expect these improvements to be of major benefit to Canadian women who in the past have not been able to participate in full numbers in these plans.
Access to pension plans for part-time workers will be provided. Generally more workers will have the opportunity to join private pension plans, and their participation in the management of their pension funds will be recognized as a right. Equal pensions for men and women retiring under identical circumstances will also be provided. Greater flexibility for workers taking early retirement will now be possible. Vesting and portability changes, as well as improvements to survivor benefits, are among the changes that will be especially satisfactory to Canadian women. The equality of women is further

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. J. Epp
recognized by the provision of splitting up pension benefits between spouses in the event of marriage breakdown.
These elements of pension reform are important not only because they improve equity and solidify the rights of workers now in pension plans, but also because they provide greater access among the workforce, especially women, to private pension plans. A great deal is left to be done in the reform of the Canada Pension Plan, but this Government believes that more Canadians will be able to contemplate a secure and rewarding retirement if they have planned previously in their working life for their retirement. These pensions reforms are a step in the direction of providing many more Canadians with the means to enjoy a secure old age with dignity.
We are acutely aware of the circumstances of older Canadians who are dependent to a greater degree on the public pension system. The decision not to modify indexation for the Guaranteed Income Supplement and veterans assistance was taken with this greater dependence in mind. I want to assure Canadians that the Government will be looking very carefully at the circumstances of these Canadians. We will monitor the adequacy of these payments and, as resources permit, they will be enriched.
This Budget asks Canadians to be realistic about the future. Everyone is asked to contribute to the restoration of sanity to our national finances. Tax increases have been contemplated as a last resort, and only because they were demanded in the circumstances in which the Government found itself. The Government has attempted, and I believe has been successful, to spread the burden of recovery as widely as possible. Business, especially the small business sector, is asked to play its part in the creation of thousands of new jobs. The stimulus given to our small businesses will enable them to grow and expand. I have no doubt that small business owners across the country, both in the commercial and in the agricultural field, will be equal to the challenge.
Governments are asked to play their part in the management of their affairs, to ensure efficiency and show leadership by example. Not least, Governments must work together, especially in the design and implementation of the new labour market strategy. The resources devoted to these training and employment programs will go farther than any previous program because of federal-provincial harmonization, local initiative and the use of the private sector as the driving force.
The Budget draws on the lessons of our history to chart a new course for the future. Canada was built on the vision and initiative of men and women who work not just for themselves, but for their children and for their communities. It would be nothing less than tragic to accept the situation of spiralling deficits that condemned our children to paying a debt they did not incur and ate away at the social infrastructure that is at the very heart of our community commitment.
Canadians elected a Government last September to show realism and compassion, blended together. No blend can be perfect. The value of this Budget is that it comes to grips with the reality of the situation and does so in a way that is fair. That is the best, the only guarantee of social security.
I say to Hon. Members that this Budget is a direct reflection of what Canadians asked us to do on September 4. I have been listening to Canadians over the last number of days since the Budget. They believe this is a response that is fair. I have been in the House for a few years. I know the immediate response to other Budgets. Other than the naysayers across the way, who already had their lines written before the Budget was even read, having already made up their mind, what is important is that Canadians wanted this direction. Canadians believe in the country. Canadians believe in their ability to invest. Canadians believe in the future. They know that future for them and for their children is best guaranteed when they have a Government that is respectful of the taxpayers' dollar and gives those Canadians the tax room and the ability to invest and develop that future. As that takes place, all of us will benefit.
Mir. Nunziata: Mr. Speaker, in his comments the Minister stated that the Budget represents advances in social policy. He referred to senior citizens and said that this will enable senior citizens to proceed through old age with dignity. He went on to say that the Budget is a direct response to what Canadians asked them to do on September 4.
Did the Minister tell Canadians, specifically senior citizens, during the election campaign that he intended to cut their pensions? Did he or his Party tell them during that election campaign that no longer would senior citizens of this country be protected against inflation? I say that the Conservative Party did not tell the Canadian people that.
I would further like to ask the Minister whom he consulted. Which senior citizens did he consult with before deciding to de-index or partially de-index the Old Age Security? Did he speak to Harold Ballard or the blue rinse set on Bay Street? He certainly did not speak to the senior citizens in York South-Weston.
Does the Minister agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who is quoted in The Toronto Star yesterday as saying that the senior citizens of this country are prepared to sacrifice in order to reduce the deficit, or does he agree with me and the Liberal Party when we say that the senior citizens of this country have sacrificed long enough and hard enough over the years? They have sacrificed for the benefit of Canadians. They have worked long and hard. They have fought in world wars and have struggled to make Canada a better place in which to live.
Why is the Minister and his Government showing complete disregard for senior citizens and plunging a great many of them into poverty because of their insensitivity by de-indexing the Old Age Security? Does that indicate caring on behalf of the Government, or does it indicate an insensitivity toward the senior citizens of this country and a disrespect for everything they have worked for and fought for?
In conclusion, where is social justice? Where is fairness when you attack the very heart of this nation? You pierce the very heart of a nation when you attack the senior citizens.
May 27, 1985

Yes, consultation took place. Yes, senior citizens understand that. Senior citizens do not want the debt to become so large and the cost of servicing the debt so great that their children and grandchildren will be forced to pay such a large portion of their incomes that they will not have the potential to buy their own homes and give educational opportunities to their children. All senior citizens understand that in order to have that kind of security, we must get our economic house in order.
The people who should stand condemned are Hon. Members opposite. Hon. Members opposite stand condemned because in 1968, the accumulated national debt was $17 billion. Today the national debt, after the Liberal legacy, is $180 billion. That is why the cost is so high today.

Mr. Speaker, among other things, I would point out to the Hon. Minister that one of the side effects of the Budget has been to disadvantage in a small way people who are blind. They will now have to pay sales taxes on dog food for their guide dogs. That is the level to which this Government is sinking. I would say to the Minister that I hope we will see that changed.
The main point I would like to make is that the $225 million that will be taken from senior citizens next year will not go to the reduction of the deficit. Not a nickel of that money will go to reduce the deficit because the Government is taking $225 million from seniors through indexing but is giving $300 million to the upper 10 per cent of taxpayers through the capital gains tax exemptions. In 1986, it will take $450 million from seniors, a group that is poor, and give $600 million through capital gains tax exemptions to a group that is extremely well off. That will go on year after year.
The speech made by the Minister was a disappointing one from a Minister of National Health and Welfare and from a man who has been known in the past to be compassionate and caring about ordinary Canadians. How is it fair to take so much from senior citizens on a pretence which is fraudulent in order to give money to the people who are receiving the benefit of the capital gains tax exemption? How can the Minister justify that inequity?

The Hon. Member is only talking about the upper 10 per cent of income earners. If he were to look at the situation of the average blue-collar worker in the United States, he would find that because of the tax incentives there, a very high percentage of blue-collar workers have invested in industry and are stockholders. The present tax structure allows only those in the corporate sector to have those advantages. Because of the new capital gains tax

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to address a few remarks to the subject of the Budget. This past weekend I convened two public meetings, one in Orillia at nine o'clock in the morning and one in Midland at two o'clock in the afternoon. There was good attendance and a great deal of interest in the Budget we brought down. I am pleased to tell the House that there has been general acceptance of the Budget and that the people of Simcoe North realize that over the past few years the Liberals had spent us into oblivion. They realized that there was a desperate situation which had to be addressed by all walks of life. The people of Simcoe North were pleased to be part of the solution to the problem rather than having to watch the problem occur as they did in the past.
There is no question that this Budget is a break with the past. If higher deficits could have created jobs, there would have been many jobs created in the country. However, we have seen higher deficits and a climbing unemployment rate under the Liberal Government. This is a break with the past. It is an opportunity for Canadians to address the deficit and to create a climate which will encourage the creation of jobs. As a result of this Budget, the estimated deficit for 1985-86 will be reduced by $4.4 billion. That is actually the third step that we took to bring our fiscal house into order.
Step one was taken last November when we brought in the expenditure reduction program. We said that the Government could cut back on what it was spending. We said that we intended to examine our expenditures in order to give Canadian taxpayers the best value for their dollar. That was universally accepted by Canadians. As a result, the investment community, our trading partners, and the international monetary community all applauded our efforts as a Government to bring our fiscal house into order.
May 27, 1985

Step two was taken last February when we introduced Estimates for our spending and borrowing, which were exactly as we said we would spend in November. Having been a Member of the House for the past six years I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberals used to bring in one set of figures which escalated by the time you saw them again. Our figures were the same in February as they were in November.
It is apparent to every Canadian that we will not reduce the deficit in one fell swoop. We need a planned program which can be defended step by step. Thai is what we are doing. We have terminated programs and projects. Over the course of the next few years we intend to reduce the number of public servants through attrition. It is important to focus on the word "attrition". We intend to examine the number of people employed by the Government and the projects in which they are employed. As people retire or resign, we will replace them with fewer people. We intend to give the Canadian people a more effective and efficient Government.
We are examining Crown corporations. We are asking whether each Crown corporation fulfils the mandate which it was given when it was created. We are asking whether there is a reason, for public policy purposes, to keep that Crown corporation and whether it is operating as efficiently as it should. That is the method through which we are attacking the deficit. We have a targeted reduction which we intend to meet over a series of years to keep faith with the Canadian people and reduce the deficit.
Another issue which is addressed as part of the Budget is job creation. Job creation was a major platform of the Government. We promised "jobs, jobs, jobs". We promised to do it by creating a climate in which jobs could be created. We did not promise that bureaucrats would create jobs. That is not a function of the bureaucracy. Bureaucracy has a definite function in External Affairs and Supply and Services, but the creation of jobs is not a function of the bureaucracy. That should be done by private enterprise. The job of the Government is to encourage businesses to invest, research, innovate, and take a chance.
The small business people who came to see me on Saturday said that they like the capital gains tax exemption. It is not that they will make a lot of money from it. Every business person in Canada who has a chance to make a dollar, knowing that he will pay only 25 cents on it, will go out and make that dollar. They are doing it now. However, through the capital gains tax exemption we want to create the perception that they can make that money and produce the jobs.
I suggest in sincerity that members of the Opposition may be missing the point. It is not the rich people who are looking forward to the capital gains tax exemption. The small business people and their employees, the backbone of the country, are the ones who are looking forward to this tax exemption because they perceive themselves to be participating in that $500,000. The rich people will pay the 25 per cent tax. This tax exemption gives every Canadian employed by small business the chance to take a chance and have a return on his or her investment.
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
Prior to the Budget we did other things to stimulate job creation in the country. We reduced federal Government expenditures, as I indicated before. We introduced Investment Canada to encourage foreign investment. It is sad to see the Liberals and New Democrats fight a Bill which would create jobs in every riding in Canada.
We have had consultation in many areas. The Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. McMillan) was in my riding consulting on the tourism business. That is the first time a Minister of Tourism did anything other than go down to Cleveland to get his picture taken on a streetcar. That is what the last joker from the Liberal Party did. We know where he is now. The Government is serious about consulting and about the tourism business in Canada.
We have changed the approach and attitude of the Department of National Revenue. That will defeat the underground economy which says it does not have to pay taxes. We are changing the attitude of the Ministry of National Revenue, which was created, fostered, and promoted by the Liberals. It cracked down on decent people. The former Minister defended that attitude, and he is gone too. Those are the steps we took before the presentation of the Budget to promote fairness and equity and to create jobs.
The consultation on the Unemployment Insurance Act is part of "creating a climate". Through consultation we will tell the business community, labour, and the bureaucracy that the Unemployment Insurance Act is not working exactly in the way we want it to. There are improvements which can be made and we will test them through consultation. That, coupled with the fact that we promised not to increase pensions, is going to help create the climate in the business community that will create jobs.
We said that we would be tough but fair. We are introducing a minimum income tax on high income Canadians. Under a series of Liberal Governments the rich people were allowed to get away without paying tax. As of our January 1 implementation date we will ensure that fairness is returned to the income tax system. I would have thought that the "holier than thou" New Democrats might have joined us in this exercise. Instead, they do not know how to handle the fact that we brought in this minimum tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You can interject any time.
Last Thursday, they sat in their seats, thunderstruck by the fairness of this Budget. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) came to the point in his speech at which he introduced a minimum tax on banks, they were thunderstruck and there was silence once again. This suggests that once again the banks have got to the New Democrats. When will they stop supporting the banks and join us in taxing the banks and trust companies? We are shocked by the way the New Democrats have abandoned their principles.
This Budget takes action for which Canadians have been asking for years. We said that there should be changes to the Pension Benefits Standard Act. The people with whom I talked at a meeting last Saturday agreed with what we are trying to do because there are people in Canada who would gladly invest but do not know exactly how to do it. They said that through expanding the vehicle of the RRSP, Canadian workers and salaried employees will be given an oportunity to invest through the RRSP mechanism. They are in favour of that. I cannot understand why the NDP is against giving workers and salaried people an opportunity to invest in this country. What could be wrong with that? Why do they take that indefensible position? Why do they not trust ordinary Canadians who want to invest in this country? It is hard to understand that lack of trust from the NDP. Other measures in this Budget include eliminating the tax shelters that existed under the former Liberal Government.
We have attempted to return fairness and equity to a system which we all support and believe can bring this country to greatness. Under the Liberals, the tax system became a haven for the rich. The system was abused as a result of the New Democrats, who do not understand the system, propping up the Liberals.
We have attempted to explain that we are in a serious situation and that we are asking all parts of the country to participate in the solution. I think the argument on fairness is valid. I do not back away from that argument for a moment. The Opposition is right to call fairness into question because the purpose of this exercise is to question the entire package.
However, when the opposition Parties talk to Canadians about the Budget I caution them to remember that any budget is a package and must be considered as a packaged proposition. I caution the Opposition seriously to consider the Budget on that basis.
I talked to a number of Canadians over the weekend. A number of Canadians also talked to my executive and campaign committee, which met for two and a half hours on Sunday morning. It is the view of those people that we have brought down a Budget with which Canadians will agree.
With respect to the budgetary process, I believe it should be addressed by all Parties in a non-partisan way. I have challenged the chartered accountant profession in my riding to review carefully the Canadian budgetary process. I believe we should review it on a non-partisan basis because for too long Governments have brought in Budgets in Canada in every month of the year. That creates problems for the business community, the professions which advise the business community and the people who work in Canada, whether they are the employers or the employees.
There is much merit to reviewing the Canadian budgetary process and asking what would suit the country. We could reach a consensus on what process would suit everyone in order to adopt a sensible process that would benefit Canadians and Parliament. Personally, I would like to see all the budget provisions passed by a certain date. I held the same view when I was in opposition. Whether or not one agrees with the provisions, the community wants certainty. While there is ample provision to argue the philosophy of a Budget as we are doing today, I believe all parliamentarians support the view that certainty in the budgetary process is important to every one of us. It is important to the people whom we represent. I ask Members of the House to consult with the professionals who advise businesses, business people and employees, in order to come up with a means to make the budgetary process work better.
I appreciate the unexpected opportunity to enter into this debate. I was simply going to question my colleagues opposite, but I appreciate this opportunity to speak.

Will the Hon. Member honestly tell us where are the fairness, justice and equity? I am sure he will agree that there is no fairness in the Budget. It is a Budget for the rich and by the rich and it attacks the poor, especially the senior citizens in the country.

Mr. Speaker, I could go on and on like this, but I feel I have conveyed the essential of my message. The Government is altogether indifferent to women's needs, as evidenced once again by the Budget it tabled last Thursday.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET'S PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fear expressed by Canadian women that the Conservative Government would sacrifice its election commitment to equality for the sake of a deficit first strategy has come true. The Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) continues past Liberal traditions of broken promises, cuts, and taxes at the expense of Canadian women and their children. Deindexing of the old age security pension will harm the most vulnerable members of Canadian society, elderly women. Over 60 per cent of them now live in poverty, and the Budget does nothing to provide relief.
For unemployed women there are no jobs. For the average women in the workforce the Budget does nothing, either. There are cuts to training programs. Lay-offs in the Public Service and privatization will hit women the hardest. There are no additional funds for the Canadian Human Rights Commission to enforce equal pay for work of equal value and employment equity.
Cuts in transfer payments to the provinces are of particular concern to women. Promised funding for child care has been ignored. Battered women will see no increase in protection from violence for themselves and their children. Canadian women who took the promise of consultation in good faith have been betrayed.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize today this Progressive Conservative Government Budget's complete disregard of the needs of Canadian women.
First of all, in the area of employment. This Government's decision to eliminate 15,000 Public Service positions will affect 5 per cent of women employed in the Public Service. The Government has implemented no special job creating scheme. Instead of fulfilling its promise to help women benefit from the technological revolution, the Government has decided to cut $78 million from training programs this year.
The Budget says nothing about part-time workers of whom 72 per cent are women. It penalizes low and medium income families through regressive sales taxes on consumer goods.
The desindexation of social programs will especially hurt people at the lower end of the economic scale who are mostly women.

subsubtopic: ELEVATION TO COLLEGE OF CARDINALS OF MONSIGNOR LOUIS-ALBERT VACHON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Rome, Pope John Paul II honoured a famous "Beauceron", and I would like to announce here in Parliament the great honour that reflects on the great riding of Beauce following the elevation to the College of Cardinals of Monsignor Louis-Albert Vachon, Archbishop of Quebec City.
Cardinal Vachon was born in 1912 in Saint-Frederic de Beauce. After a life dedicated to others in his capacity as priest and as Rector of Laval University for many years, he was made Archbishop of Quebec City and Primate of the Catholic Church in Canada, and today, a cardinal.

May 27, 1985
Throughout his life he has been an example to us, reflecting the basic values that are part of our heritage in Beauce. Truly great men do not tolerate mediocrity, and many Beaucerons have, like him, aimed for excellence and achieved it.
He reached his goals through hard work and sheer tenacity. He is an honoured member of his community, and today, the entire Christian and Catholic community of Canada, Quebec and Beauce is honoured to have him in their midst.
His appointment to the highest post in the Catholic Church gives us cause for rejoicing as a community. Again, I am indeed honoured to be able to pay tribute to this famous Beauceron, His Eminence Cardinal Louis-Albert Vachon.

subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF MINIMUM TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past federal election campaign the Progressive Conservative Party pledged to improve the fairness of our tax system by introducing a minimum personal income tax. That tax will take effect on January 1, 1986. The date was chosen to allow for consultation and to avoid, as much as possible, any adverse effects on farmers, people starting new businesses, and retired people living on fixed incomes from dividends. Adverse effects could very well result from such a major tax change midway through the taxation year.
Opposition Parties have expressed concern that the minimum tax did not take effect as of the budget date of May 23. This is most surprising, bearing in mind their well-known sense of fair play and equity. I am sure that upon quiet reflection opposition Parties will enthusiastically agree the Government has not only kept its word but has chosen the best, fairest, and fastest way of implementing the minimum tax.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-IMPACT ON ELDERLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Prime Minister Mulroney made a solemn commitment during the election campaign-he was not going to tamper with social programs, especially old age security pensions. As the Progressive Conservative Leader himself put it at the time, it was a sacred trust.
Well, Prime Minister Mulroney has failed to live up to that solemn commitment and, among people most penalized by the Mulroney-Wilson Budget, we must include the senior citizens of Canada who between now and 1990-91 stand to lose $4.5
billion as a result of the 3 per cent old age security desindexation.
Since 2.5 million elderly Canadian men and women receive pensions, it means that each senior citizen will lose $1,800 between now and 1990-91. The Mulroney-Wilson Budget amounts to a direct attack against the purchasing power of elderly Canadians, for they will have to do with $54 less a month in 1990-91. Is it fair to expect men and women aged 65 or more to carry such a burden while multinational oil companies will be getting $2.5 billion in 1990-91 alone?
The Mulroney-Wilson Budget is unfair to millions of taxpayers and even more so to older people, most of whom have nothing else but their old age security cheques to make ends meet. Old age security pensions will be reduced by $54 a month in 1990-91, and that is unfair to the elderly to whom Prime Minister Mulroney promised during the election campaign that social programs, and especially old age pensions, would not be tampered with.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-OBJECTIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Government was elected on a platform for change, and on that basis we have charted a course of action to create jobs, growth and increased Government responsibility.
Since November, over 200,000 real jobs were created, and this Budget is to be an effective tool for creating jobs for Canadians. It will reduce the deficit inherited from the previous Liberal Government by the end of the decade, without compromising economic renewal, and it contains proposals for more effective management of government operations.
The Budget proposals encourage private initiative and private sector growth. These measures represent a fundamental break with the past. For instance, this Government is proposing a life-time capital gains exemption of $500,000 for each Canadian, a measure aimed at encouraging Canadians to invest in small and large businesses, which will help stimulate the economy and counter the effects of the underground economy.

subsubtopic: SEXUAL HARASSMENT COMPLAINT-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last week it became public that the Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester was the subject of a complaint to the Canadian Human Rights Commission. My colleague, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston, called for greater confidentiality at the commission. But on Friday the Solicitor General took a totally different tack. He actually took sides in the case, saying he was doing it as a Minister and a friend of his former Cabinet colleague. He rejected the evidence even though he admitted not having seen it. Does the Prime Minister not feel that his Solicitor General showed poor judgment in taking sides in a case before a federal commission?
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Justice and Attorney
General of Canada): Mr. Speaker, as I am the Minister who answers for the Human Rights Commission let me say that many Hon. Members of Parliament have expressed some disquiet with respect to certain aspects of the policy of the Human Rights Commission relating to complaints which are unsubstantiated accusations at that particular stage in the process. The same kinds of views have been expressed before the House of Commons justice committee. We are considering possible amendments to the Human Rights Commission legislation at the present time, and this is one of the areas which will have to be considered.
I am sure that all Hon. Members of this House realize the perils with which people in public life are faced in this kind of situation. My colleague was expressing his concern in that area, and I believe it is a concern which we all have to consider.

The Minister of Justice is throwing us a red herring. I am not talking about the procedures of the commission. That is fair game for legislators. What the Solicitor General did in this case was to challenge the evidence, and say he didn't believe the evidence against his former colleague even though he had not seen the evidence. I want to ask the Prime Minister again, because it is a question about the Cabinet not about the Human Rights Commission, does the Prime Minister continue to have confidence in a Solicitor General who would take sides and challenge the impartiality of the commission like this?

Mr. Speaker, I construed the comments of the Solicitor General as comments of concern about the procedure which could affect any Hon. Member of this House, in much the same way as the Hon. Member for York South-Weston indicated his concern about the same kind of problem. Inasmuch as it is a quasi-judicial process I would not want to go beyond that except to say that I thought that the Hon. Member for York South-Weston
and the Solicitor General were expressing a concern about injustices which could flow from the procedures themselves.

subsubtopic: SPACE BASED NAVIGATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext: What is the government's current participation in developing space based navigational satellite systems?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: SPACE BASED NAVIGATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEMS
speechtext:
1 am
informed by the Departments of National Defence, Regional Industrial Expansion and Transport as follows:

May 27, 1985
Order Paper Questions
Canada through the Department of National Defence has been involved with the NAVSTAR Global Positioning System (GPS) since 1978. This is the NATO endorsed space based navigation system which is being developed and funded entirely by the U.S. military. Canada and nine other NATO nations provide personnel and funds for a NATO Project Office at Space Division in Los Angeles. To date, DND has expended $380,000 and provided two officers to the project office and total cost is not expected to exceed $980,000 when the present agreement terminates at the end of 1988.
When NAVSTAR GPS becmes fully operational in 1988 it will meet the majority of military navigation requirements. It also will be available to civil users. Offshore resource exploration, hydrographic and geophysical surveying, and maritime navigation are but a few areas where the system has great potential.
Canadian Marconi Company is currently being assisted via the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion's Defence Industry Productivity Program (DIPP) in the development of NAVSTAR/GPS receiver technology. The development program comprises three areas:
(1)	the exploration and implementation of several areas of technology common to all types of receiver;
(2)	the development of the market/product potential for low-cost, moderate performance receivers suitable for military and commercial transport aircrafts and ships;
(3)	the development of the market/product potential of a highly accurate and versatile receiver suitable for geodetic, surveying and positioning applications.
This DIPP assisted development program started in 1981 and is anticipated to be completed in 1986. Expenditures to date are in the amount of $484,070. Total expenditures upon completion of contract will be approximately $3,075,000.
Transport Canada has through the issuance of a Canadian Airspace Systems Plan indicated that the present ground based navigational system will continue as the navigational guidance system for civil aviation aircraft flying in Canada until at least the year 2000.
Presently the International Civil Aviation Organization is addressing the issue of future navigation system including the option of a satellite based system in the early 2000s as part of a new committee FANS (Future Air Navigations Systems).
The Canadian Air Transportation Administration as a member of this committee heads the Canadian delegation.
Transport Canada is also involved in the following activities:
(i)	participation in the U.S.-based consultative agency developing standards and techniques for the future NAVSTAR/ Global Positioning System in the Differential Mode, which is of interest to special marine and offshore industry users,
(ii)	evaluation, under contract, of differential NAVSTAR/ GPS for Coast Guard missions such as buoy positioning and
(iii)	technical supervision of DRIE-sponsored contract to Canadian Marconi Company for development of low cost civil air and marine NAVSTAR/GPS receiver.

The mukluks have been exchanged for the Bay Street boots, but when one looks beyond the PR and the pizzaz, Tory policies are still policies of restraint, increased taxes and high unemployment. The policies are the same in Ottawa as they are in British Columbia. I note the similarity to the policies in the United Kingdom which I visited recently, and the results of those policies are devastating.

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Ms. Mitchell
There is no question that the new Government, and especially the new Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), are more slick and perhaps more slippery than they were in the Joe Clark days.
