subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course, I am referring to the characteristics of the Government. The participants at the Summit Conference, particularly the representatives of consumer groups, labour groups and women's organizations, unanimously wanted a "jobs first" priority. This was quite evident on television every day.
The Prime Minister pretended to listen very seriously, and I am sure those groups believed that their views would have some impact. However, the Budget reveals that it was his corporate friends to whom he was really listening. There are no funds for job creation provided in the Budget. The unemployed are completely ignored, as if they did not exist in this country. The Budget caters to the corporate sector with capital gain gifts, tax loopholes and a $2 billion bonanza for oil companies.
Middle income earners and the poor will bear the brunt of the increased sales tax, including taxes on health products and energy conservation products, as well as a nine-cent per gallon gas tax.
As the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) pointed out in his statement today, if one adds the increased cost of taxes and the reduction on indexation in this Budget to the increases of some $500 that were implemented last fall, average families will pay $1,000 more this year. This is not only a burden upon families. It is also a burden upon small businesses, the very sector in which the Government professes to put all its faith for job creation. How can small businesses survive, expand and employ more people if consumer demand is down? With $1,000 less to spend, surely that will happen.
1 challenge Tory Members in the House today to convince me and the women of Canada-and I hope they will do so in the question and comment period-that the Budget is not anti-women. Canadian women, who earn on average 60 per cent of men's wages, will pay $1,000 extra in taxes or reduced benefits. Increasing numbers of women are sole supporters of their children and are on very low incomes, if not already on welfare. There is no job creation targeted for women in the Budget. Indeed, training funds are being reduced. Women are faced with being displaced or phased out, either entirely or in part-time jobs, by technological change. This is the time when they need retraining opportunities, new job creation and alternative kinds of work. There are no funds allocated in the Budget to employment equity, the Government's own program which it introduced and in which it presumably believed. There is nothing to increase funds for the Human Rights Commission.
Cuts in public services, privatization which will go along with phasing out Crown corporations, and the contracting out of all these techniques, will have a proportionately greater impact on women because they are the last hired and the first fired and they are in the lowest paid clerical and service positions. They will be the ones who will not have jobs. They will be the ones who will be in part-time work. They are the ones about whom the Government does not care. It did not do anything about the prorated benefits for part-time workers. Of course, elderly women will continue in poverty because public pension reforms, which are so desperately needed, have been ignored.
As the Hon. Member for Vancouver East, I must say that we in British Columbia know from experience the devastating impact of a tough, deficit-reducing, Conservative restraint Budget. In British Columbia, experience shows that restraint has resulted in a chronic unemployment rate of 15 per cent. Skilled people have been unemployed for two or more years now. Also, it has resulted in chops in essential services such as educational, health and social services. Failures of small businesses have resulted rather than increases of new enterprises which the Government thinks will occur by some magic.
May 27, 1985

There is a lack of job creation and economic planning, particularly in the resource sectors, as is the case now. There are high costs as a result of increased violence, crime and social stress which go along with high unemployment and low incomes. The B.C. experience proves that Conservative economic policy, whether it is the Progressive Conservative Party federally or the Social Credit Party in British Columbia, simply does not work. Even Conservative business people, people who supported the Social Credit in British Columbia, are saying that the economy has been stultified, that we need change, and that this is not the way to go. The Fraser Institute is somewhat apologetic, and there is absolutely no evidence that the private sector, if left to do these things, will automatically create jobs when there is this kind of oppression in the economy. The federal Conservative Budget will add another layer of hardship on B.C. residents and on the residents of other provinces, particularly those in eastern Canada. There is no increase in job creation to help alleviate the high unemployment rate. Ordinary citizens will pay more in taxes.
No funds are budgeted for the ailing forestry and fishery industries, for housing or for municipal development. Even shipbuilding subsidies are being cut, which concerns me in my riding of Vancouver East. Revenues which should have been taxed from the wealthy are now lost because of the removal of the capital gains tax and other tax loopholes. The temporary minimum surtax is a laugh. We wanted a real, effective 20 per cent minimum tax. This is what the Prime Minister promised and has neglected to enforce.
Public services will also be cut back federally and Crown corporations will be privatized. In British Columbia we know that this will mean a lack of services, inadequate services, a loss of jobs and reduced social conditions with increased costs of health, educational and social services. A $2 billion cut in transfer payments, which one sees if one reads carefully the small print in the Budget, is a very, very serious concern. I hope very much that there will be a mass move to ensure that this does not happen. It will definitely worsen the situation in my province. The Budget is bad news for Canada generally and it is double bad news for British Columbia.
I would like to refer to the particular impact of this Budget on areas of social policy. What will the Conservatives do now in the area of health and social services to improve the general well-being of Canadians, especially the well-being of poor Canadians and of women? As I have said and will keep on saying, the lack of new funds for job creation is really difficult to believe. It condemns many thousands of Canadians to chronic unemployment, to the insecurity, stress and poverty of years ahead, not to mention the high cost of maintaining people on social programs and unemploynment.
It is not only the lack of money which concerns us. Of course money is the basic cause, but it is the absolute dwindling of self-confidence which occurs when persons go day after day lookind for work, submitting resumes, feeling that they are losing their skills and their employability, feeling that they cannot remain competitive, and feeling worthless and angry. We know that when there is lots of anger, it leads to
The Budget-Ms. Mitchell
violence. In society today we have an increase in family violence and abuse of children, which I am sure is not unrelated to high unemployment. What is more, there is the lack of opportunity for a whole generation of young people.
All of us in the House say this day after day, but I hope we really feel it. It is not only the lack of jobs, it is the lack of opportunity for the future which is really so depressing. On top of that of course, there are the cuts which have occurred in education, training a work-related experiences. Again the federal Government is neglecting to increase shared funding in the Budget for these areas.
I think it is immoral of this Government to have turned its back on the unemployed, and it was hypocritical of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who had the gall to say: "This Budget is about jobs".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that Members are touchy when there are direct quotes. The quote I read is that this Budget is about jobs. I will leave it to the Hon. Member to interpret that in her own conscience.
In his Budget, the Minister of Finance went on to say that they are going to cut 15,000 jobs in the public service. A lot more jobs will be cut because of privatization and doing away with Crown corporations. That is quite obvious.
A similar kind of misleading of the public in budget policies is evident in the statement by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) who said that their priority is to be Canadians with the greatest need. I challenge the Conservative Members to prove this. I assume those Canadians with the greatest need are the low-income Canadians. However, they are the hardest hit by this Budget. Not only are they being whacked with $1,000 in extra taxes, but their family benefits will be affected as well. There is a slight, token increase in the child tax credit for the lowest-income people, but that is about one-tenth of the actual extra cost they will be forced to pay with the extra taxes.
As my colleagues have said, and others will elaborate, the limit on the indexation of Old Age Security may not sound much to seniors right now, but if you look at the cumulative effect, it is a very serious and unfair policy. I am told by the social policy reform group that by 1987 this will mean a cumulative loss of about $1,577 for a single pensioner. By 1990, they will lose $537 in one year. That is what this reduction of indexation of old age pensions means.
The indexation on family allowance is also being limited. This is contrary to what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said twice in the House today. It is an erosion of universality. The Liberals tried this trick. They kept eroding family allowances and other social benefits by not indexing them fully. As a result, the real value of those benefits has gone down over the years. Therefore, it is a real erosion of univerality in both cases.
The child tax exemption for older children, those who are going on to post-secondary education, will also be restricted. For low-income families, those earning under $22,000, there is a slight increase in the child tax credit, but far less than we recommended in the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. We spent weeks talking to witnesses and doing other work among ourselves. Surely even the Conservative Members will admit that that was a wasted effort. They did not pay any attention to it. This year an extra $70 will be given in the child tax credit. However, this will be taken away because of the increase in the sales tax. Most witnesses who appeared before us in committee advocated removal of the
regressive child tax exemption. Conservative Members seem to be in favour of this. I am sure my colleague, the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) will agree that most of the witnesses were in favour of this. There was nothing in the report that advocated the kind of cut-back that comes out in this Budget.
According to the social policy reform group, the changes in this family benefit package that are evident in this Budget mean a loss of $400 million from the child benefit package. That $400 million is being taken away from Canada's children. Therefore, you cannot say the children are not victims of government cuts. By 1990, all families will be net losers under the child benefit package.
I want to concentrate my remaining time on what this Budget means or does not mean for Canadian women. Will it take them a step closer to equality in the workplace? Cutting 15,000 public service jobs will have a disproportionate impact on women, as will selling off Crown corporations and moves towards privatization. Women will largely be the victims. They will be left unprotected, with non-unionized part-time jobs with inadequate benefits. We only have to look at what Air Canada is doing in trying to promote unlimited part-time jobs to see that this is the way things will go in Canada. Our Government should not be encouraging that.
The Government has taken no steps to require prorated benefits for part-time workers, most of whom are women. There should have been amendments to the Canada Pension Plan as well as for private pensions. Although they are minimal, we certainly support the changes that are suggested, as far as they go, for public servants. The Government made no reference to employment equity programs. As I said earlier, the Canadian Human Rights Commission must have more money to enforce the employment equity provisions.
I could go on. I will conclude by saying that the cuts in transfer payments will not only be cuts to the provinces. They are basic cuts to new programs, including child care which desperately needs funding. The Prime Minister said the problem is urgent. As will, it means cuts to health care; really to a new kind of health care, community health care, which in the Throne Speech this Government said it was committed to. In its election promises, it even put a figure of $150 million on reforming the health system, with more emphasis on community health prevention.
I wish I had time to outline the budget proposals which the New Democratic Party developed after weeks of discussion and visits to over 24 centre across Canada. Unlike the Liberals, who offered no alternatives, and who have a despicable record, we developed a jobs first proposal. We have a jobs first proposal with many recommendations that are practical. We show how they can be paid for. We do not believe that the deficit is the first priority. People must be the first priority. It means that job strategy must be the first priority of this Government. It means federal leadership, public leadership. In the short-term, funds are required to create meaningful community jobs so that people can be fulfilled, use their skills and have a secure future. Then our country would truly be more productive.
May 27, 1985

Mr. Speaker, as a woman in this Government I feel personally offended by the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). We, the women in this Government, have worked very hard to represent our sisters across Canada. This Budget will be helpful to them. Her remarks were very offensive. It will be helpful because up until now women have had to live with temporary jobs created by emergency measures. Those jobs, if they were lucky, lasted about 20 weeks. They were then back on welfare. We want to stop this vicious circle. This is why this Budget has been shaped in this way. We want jobs to be created by the small business sector in our communities, the most vital job creation sector in our country.
In my riding of Gatineau, which is in the Outaouais, the small business sector is the most dynamic sector in that part of Quebec. Like the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), this past weekend I was in my riding. I spoke to small business-people, many of whom are women who have managed to create small businesses in the area. They are very pleased with this Budget because at last they will be able to create permanent jobs. They were sick and tired of these temporary job-creation programs.
I would also like to remind the Hon. Member for Vancouver East of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said in Question Period today, that 89,000 jobs were created in April, 60 per cent of which were for women. That is a fact as well. I would also like to remind her that the training allowance in the Budget of $900 million for 1986-87, the same as it is in this year's Budget, will give better allowances for women who go on training. Up until now allowances were not sufficient for women because they have extra expenses that men who have women at home looking after the children do not have. That too will be an improvement of the women's lot.
I would also like to remind her that at the request of the labour sector, which she purports to represent, we will now allow a deduction for contribution to the-

-Solidarity Fund of Quebec.

That will go a long way toward restoring jobs for women who are being laid off in small industries and in the forestry sector in the Outaouais and Abitibi. That is a very positive thing for the women of Canada.
I would also like to remind the Hon. Member that there will be access for homemakers to the pension plan after discussions are terminated with the provinces. That is something that must happen before it can be put in the Budget. Quebec has signalled that it is interested in finding a formula so that women who stay at home because they want to bring up their families at home will be able to.
I hope that women will have the right to choose the way of life they want. They do not have to listen to the Hon. Member for Vancouver East, living only the way she thinks is the right
The Budget-Ms. Mitchell
way for women to live. That is the other thing that offends me. She talks about taking away the total deduction for couples when the woman stays at home. She is dictating to the women of Canada the lifestyle that they should lead, and I object to that. I think women will be equal the day they can decide how best they want to live without being punished for the choices they make.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say to the Hon. Member opposite that I would hope that she would be an advocate for women, and I think from some of the things she was saying that she possibly is an advocate for women. I would hope that she would not be offended by some of us believing very strongly in and working very hard at being advocates as well, as that is our job.
I wish I could ask the Hon. Member some of the questions she asked me. Of course we do not want 20-week jobs. No one has ever suggested that we want 20-week jobs. I have certainly never said that. I want long-term jobs but I do not think that the only way to get long-term jobs is through some magic worked by the private sector and small businesses while small businesses themselves are saying that they simply do not have the kind of consumer demand to do so. I do not really see what she is getting at.
I think it will be great if many more jobs are created by small business. We would all like that. We need millions of jobs in this country. However, that will not happen overnight, as the Minister has said and I am taking into account the first-hand experience we have had in British Columbia. As well, I just returned from Britain. The job situation over there is so dreadful that Conservative Members are splitting from the Margaret Thatcher position. I really do not have any great confidence that this approach will work.
We are all for jobs and we are all for small business. I hope, though, that as an advocate for women and as an advocate for small business, the Hon. Member will be doing something very dramatic to persuade the Government to make it possible for women in business to have more access to credit. It is disgusting that nothing has been done about that.
The Hon. Member raised the matter of the training allowances. Women's organizations and others have been fighting for years to have more adequate provisions for women. I congratulate the Government for putting this in place. It is

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Ms. Mitchell
doing a better job in some areas than the Liberal Government did. However, there is not enough. What is the point of having some improvement in benefits if the women cannot get into those training programs? I have heard from women right across the country who indicate that they cannot get into nontraditional jobs. They are being phased out of traditional jobs in many instances and cannot get into training programs or pre-employment programs that will help give them equal access to non-traditional jobs, and that is a fact. If the Hon. Member could figure out some way to help that situation, more power to her.
Regarding the question of choice, I really did not understand what the Hon. Member was saying when she accused me of trying to restrict the choices of women. That is the last thing I would ever do. I believe in complete freedom of choice; not only in freedom of choice, but in the opportunities that allow women to have a choice. I believe women should have enough income that they can choose to remain at home or go into the workforce if that is their choice. I also believe, and I hope she does as well, in freedom of choice as far as reproductive rights are concerned. That is something on which the Government has taken no position. I very much fear that if it did take a position it would be a negative one.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not expect to do as the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) asked us to do earlier, that is to persuade her of something. She knows as do I that we begin with fundamentally different philosophies and ideologies. Her view is that the Government ought to be doing for the people everything that she can imagine needs to be done. The fact of the matter is that in her request for more jobs, reasonable as it is, she fails to recognize that the approach that she is advocating is precisely the approach utilized by the Liberals for most of the last 15 or 16 years. That is an approach of extending the debt and presuming that the Government, through some make-work program, will put in place jobs that are real. That approach has proven to be a dismal failure.
The fact is that in the approach that has been taken since September, 1984, there has been to date 210,000 jobs created, 89,000 of them since April and 60 per cent of which were for women. That is in considerable contrast to what was put forth by Opposition Parties when they indicated that the November 28 statement would cost 50,000 jobs.
What we must recognize fundamentally is that there is a significant and basic philosophical difference in the approaches to creating jobs. Surely the Hon. Member should find no objection to putting in place a system that creates permanent jobs, a system that allows the thrill of the entrepreneurial mentality to go forward and be productive, a system that allows business to hire people who will remain permanently hired as opposed to having the Government create jobs by having people paint churches, fix fences and clean up roadsides.
When the Hon. Member indicates that the Minister is hypocritical because he had said that the Budget was about jobs, jobs, jobs and then cuts Crown corporations, which she then relates to hypocrisy, she is basically supporting the notion
that the debt should continue. Where does she find within her reflection on this matter that it is productive for Canada to continue having one out of three tax dollars doing nothing more than paying for the interest on the accumulated debt? If the debt were gone, the Government could do 30 per cent more for all the social services of Canada. We could have 30 per cent more for hospitals, airports and virtually everything for which the Government spends money.

Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure what were his specific questions, but I will comment on his comments.
I disagree with the Member that what we are proposing is the same as the Liberals. I agree with the Member that the major focus on job creation, with some exceptions, was on short-term, make-work projects which recycled people on and off unemployment insurance benefits. While those projects were not entirely a waste of money, they were not productive as far as creating something new was concerned. Often, people felt abused by that system.
In our report, Canada Unlimited, we made 70 recommendations to create meaningful and productive work. The report also places a great emphasis on enterprises, not only on small business, which we agree certainly generates jobs, but also on co-operative endeavours. The report recommended more startup funds, low interest loans and so on to help start workers' cooperatives. That is something to which I hope the Government would give more emphasis. One of the Liberal programs which was fairly good in that endeavour was LEAP. That was a three-year program which helped people to develop skills as well as to set up non-profit enterprises.
I cannot agree with the assumption in the question the Hon. Member asked me about the national debt. Of course, we do not want things to continue as they are. Our Party wants, as much as the Government, to bring down the national debt. But, it must be done in a sensible manner in order that people will not be hurt. It cannot be done in the way in which it was done in British Columbia. For heaven's sake, the Hon. Member should visit British Columbia to see what has been done to the people there. That system has abused people, created hardships and added to unemployment rolls, social assistance rolls and health costs. It has destroyed families. We should do it in a manner which will give some public leadership and encourage the private sector to do as much as possible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate. I have enjoyed all the comments which have been made by colleagues to date.
At the present time the spending of the federal Government accounts for roughly 67 per cent of the total economic activity in New Brunswick, my province. Most of the expenditures are
May 27, 1985

in the form of payments to the provincial Government and to individuals. The level of dependency on federal expenditures in New Brunswick is shared proportionately by all Atlantic Provinces. That dependency is the result of federal policies which have been practised over the last 20 years, and it leaves the Province of New Brunswick and other Atlantic Provinces in a fragile and tragic position.
I would like to emphasize that the industrial policies which were practised by the former administration did much more to maintain incomes and employment in other parts of Canada than they did in New Brunswick and other Atlantic Provinces. Federal subsidies to de Havilland and Canadair alone have been greatly in excess of the sums paid for any industrial development program in the Atlantic Provinces since World War II. The rate of unemployment in New Brunswick is a stain on the conscience of the nation. The level of wages is two-thirds of the national average and the resource-based economy is extremely vulnerable to international and national cyclical downturns.
The basic characteristics of New Brunswick and the Atlantic econoy in the mid-1980s are: resource-based industries; a good record in job creation out-stripped by more people looking for work, resulting in higher unemployment than nationally; lower personal incomes, especially earned incomes; higher levels of federal transfer payments to individuals, with unemployment benefits assuming increasing importance; lower levels of private investment; higher levels of government spending and employment; higher levels of federal transfers to other Governments, and declining levels of trageted regional development spending, to a point where they are a small fraction of increased unemployment insurance transfers.
In summary, at the present time the economies of New Brunswick and other Atlantic Provinces are much too dependent on the flow of federal transfer payments. Strong new policies to expand the industrial base of New Brunswick and other Atlantic Provinces will bring great benefits to both the regional economy and the economy of Canada as a whole. To achieve that goal is the challenge that faces our Government. The severe economic problems that face our nation do not make it easy to meet that challenge.
For a moment, I would like to look at the expenditures in New Brunswick to see if they could not be re-allocated to generate more economic growth and help put in place a badly needed private sector economy.
DREE expenditures in 1971 dollars declined from $145 million in 1972 to $45 million in 1982. I suggest that other evidence of a reduced commitment toward the importance of regional development can be seen with the relative proportions of spending in other regional development programs over the past decade.
During the past decade, the federal Government spent $412 million in New Brunswick for projects associated with regional development. That is roughly equal to the $440 million paid to Canadair in two years. Those pay-outs are insignificant compared with the $1.4 billion which was written off at Canadair by the Canadian taxpayers.
The Budget-Mr. Howie
Regional development expenditures have been reducing in Atlantic Canada as unemployment expenditures have been increasing. In 1972, DREE expenditures were 67 per cent of unemployment insurance payments. By 1982, the reduced DREE expenditures were 10 per cent of unemployment insurance payments.
The complexion of federal expenditures in New Brunswick and other Atlantic Provinces has been more like foreign aid and mere spending than economic assistance and investment. The balance is wrong. We must change the balance to foster more economic development.
Private sector stimulation will be necessary if our smaller private sector is to be the engine of economic growth. Enhanced and improved regional development programs that provide long-term job opportunities for Atlantic Canadians are essential if we wish to reduce dependence on the federal Treasury and increase the long-term economic viability of our region.
Federal policies to promote regional economic development should be concerned primarily with expanding the industrial base of the region. Economic problems of the region cannot permanently be solved by transfer payments or by a dependence on high expenditures by the federal Government.
If Atlantic Canada is going to compete, we must ensure that our incentives are adequate. Our private sector is underdeveloped and so are the capital markets. If Atlantic Canadian industries are going to be established, grow and prosper, we must create a climate that is attractive to industry. The federal Government's policy of reducing interest rates is a major step in that direction.
Proposals to develop freer trade are attractive to Atlantic Canadians whose products seek expanding United States markets. Programs to improve productivity are another major step in that direction.
I would like to mention some of the things which the Government has done recently to move in the direction of which I have been speaking.
Federal support for the establishment and expansion of Process Technology Ltd., in my constituency, is a major step in the diversification of the economy, with special emphasis on non-resource-based manufacturing. Process Technology embodies new technologies and is the flagship of the high technology industry in the Province of New Brunswick.
The province possesses a number of strengths which can be the basis for growth opportunities in the development of products and services embodying new technologies. These include the New Brunswick Research and Productivity Council which has attracted worldwide attention for its work in metallurgy; a well established engineering school at the University of New Brunswick, which offers the only Ph. D. in North America in computer assisted design and manufacturing; and excellent schools of computer science and world class expertise in telecommunications technology. The use of CAD/

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Howie
CAM techniques, being assisted by the province's manufacturing technology centre, has the potential to greatly improve the competitive position of small companies. My Government has just given the New Brunswick Research and Productivity Council a $4.2 million grant for that purpose.
It is important to improve the over-all productivity and competitive position of New Brunswick's industries. The leading industry in New Brunswick which provides the largest number of jobs is the forest industry. The Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) has just announced a $35 million contribution to the forestry complex being located in Fredericton which will open a unique window on research for the entire forest industry in the region. This will greatly enhance the transfer of new technology to industry and expand the research and development component for this vital industry.
The availability of unskilled and semi-skilled labour provides a challenge for Government to provide needed facilities now in order to stimulate employment now. The announcement by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle) of the commence of construction this year of "J" Division Headquarters of the RCMP in Fredericton-a $20 million project-is a step in this direction.
The need to increase added value in New Brunswick products by increasing the level of processing the New Brunswick resources is another important strategy and a worthy strategic objective. The announcement by my Government of its $42 million participation in the development of the REPAP paper mill project on the Miramichi, which will produce a high grade of lightweight coated paper to be sold largely in the United States, is an example of putting your money where your mouth is. The retention of the military base on the Miramichi is another objective achieved by this Government.
Another major industry in New Brunswick, which at the moment is underdeveloped, is tourism. The Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. McMillan) in this Government has recently implemented a federal-provincial program involving $22 million federal dollars and $10 million provincial for this very purpose. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre) has signed a joint agreement with his New Brunswick counterpart to improve and increase purchasing in that province. Jobs are the number one priority of this Government and the $60 million development of the Canadian Forces Base at Gagetown already announced by my Government will help provide them.
The new course of action for 1985-1986 commits Canada and New Brunswick to pursuing measures undertaken in existing subsidiary agreements and to undertake new joint measures in support of economic development in New Brunswick. Two of these, an ERDA subsidiary agreement for industrial development and a subsidiary agreement for industrial innovation and technology development, are expected to be signed in the near future. Premier Hatfield and Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) also agreed to assess where supplemental measures may be required for certain regions of New Brunswick. Current plans indicate that both Governments will expend an estimated $93 million in total in New Brunswick under existing agreements during 1985-1986.
It is crucially important to New Brunswick, which sells more to New England than it does to other eastern Canadian provinces, that Canada's trade policy emphasize the development and maintenance of positive trade relations with the United States with the aim of reducing obstacles to increased trade flows.
There are other challenges which face us. Because of its dispersed population and heavy dependence on exports, and to a lesser extent, central Canadians markets, the quality and costs of transportation services are crucial to New Brunswick's economic development. As just one example, an assessment for Transport Canada indicated that New Brunswick would be the most adversely affected of the four Atlantic Provinces by the removal of freight rate subsidies now provided under the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act. Recent announcements concerning freight rate subsidies by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski), who understands our problems, the reintroduction of the Atlantic Limited rail passenger train service and the continuation of the dayliner between Fredericton and Saint John, indicate that we have a Government which will listen and respond to our needs. It gives us the confidence that our problems will be addressed.
The upgrading of highways in the northern and eastern regions of the province to an all-weather standard has been a major federal priority. This work is now nearing completion and has succeeded in reducing the cost of moving resource exports to markets and improving the linkages between the northern regions and the urban centres of the south.
It may now be appropriate to consider how transportation measures can be used to improve the linkages between the complementary business functions distributed among the major urban centres; Saint John, manufacturing and port; Moncton, distribution and business services; and Fredericton, public administration, education and research. The upgrading, and in some cases, realignment of the highway link between the three centres represents one such approach.
There may also be opportunities now with the new federal airline deregulation policy to achieve improved air service between the major New Brunswick centres and between New Brunswick urban centres and other Maritime cities. As well, a third level air carrier service, for example, if established between New Brunswick centres, might make feasible improved service to the important New England market. Potentially, such improved air service could reduce the cost of doing business and greatly increase the attractiveness of a New Brunswick location for secondary manufacturing and services industry.
Another important issue in the transportation area relates to the ability of the port of Saint John to undertake the investment required for it to maintain its competitive position. The port is still heavily in debt from the expansion program undertaken in the 1970s and is not currently in a position to finance new investments. The existing debt load has prevented the port from obtaining local port commission status, as the new federal policy requires that a port demonstrate financial
May 27, 1985

self-sufficiency in order to be eligible. However, the port urgently requires new facilities such as a roll-on-roll-off service, to improve its competitive position. Such a facility would benefit New Brunswick exporters through reduction in handling costs and through an increase in the availability and quality of shipping services.
The resource based economies of the northern counties of New Brunswick have helped close the gap in employment income per capita with the provincial average which was made possible in part by federal-provincial programs.
Another factor behind the growth in the economies of the Madawaska, Gloucester and Kent Counties, has been the emergence of small manufacturing firms established by local entrepreneurs and selling primarily on regional and national markets. This underscores the importance of a small business incentive program. It also underlines the key thrust of this budget. The budget stimulates the small business sector, which is the engine of jobs, by creating more potential pools of capital, more generous research and development incentives and an attractive capital gains tax exemption. With a realistic and balanced medium-term strategy, the Minister now controls the deficit without threatening economic recovery, social programs or job-creation, while ensuring significant deficit reductions later.
The federal Government has been acting in a spirit of national conciliation and co-operation throughout its short term in office. It has attempted to put its house in order, to create a climate that is attractive to industry. It has also attempted to increase its ability to help regions of the country which suffer from disparities.
I reject the claim of Hon. Members of the Opposition who speak of sneaky and dishonest tax increases. Nothing could be sneakier than crippling the government's ability to deliver necessary services by strangling it in its own debt. We have had enough of grandiose announcements and constant shifts in direction which have created major problems with investor and consumer confidence over the past few years. This budget points out the direction rather than pretends we can do everything in one fell swoop. The corollary to that, the budget has planned the gradual phase-out of many loopholes in the taxation system and in programs. After all, these were legitimate deductions to which persons were properly entitled and they are entitled the reasonable notice of their discontinuance. That is what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is giving.
Significantly, major issues involving social policy are not decided unilaterally or arbitrarily by the federal Government because they involve the provinces. Our Government is under no illusion that it is going to be easy to get us out of the mess the previous Government put us into. But this Budget does point in a new direction; it is a break with the past and a serious effort to maximize the delivery of quality service at the lowest possible cost.
Some of our opponents refer to the Budget as gutless. I reject that allegation. By putting its credibility on the line, by
The Budget-Mr. Henderson
saying it trusts the private sector to make wise decisions, by making no attempt to hide its direction, the Government has indicated it will stand or fall by what it believes in. This is an example of political courage which is so rare that some of our opponents appear unable to recognize it for what it is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to listen to the speech of my friend from New Brunswick, the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), you would think that all is well in Atlantic Canada. But I do not think that is the case.
First I would like to address the issue which has been on the minds of Canadians since Thursday, and that issue is jobs. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said this Budget was about jobs. Well, I say to you that this Budget is not at all about jobs in Atlantic Canada, and I do not think it is about jobs in Canada as a whole. Fewer dollars will be spent, as I read this Budget, on training and job creation. So how can the Government claim that the priority goal is jobs for Canadians? Where are all those jobs we were told about by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance? As I say, I have not seen them in the Budget plans.
There is a plan, of course, to free up the entrepreneurial spirit, and we on this side, and I think all Members of the House, agree that there is an engine of growth there, but we have to consider those areas of the country where it is very difficult to get the entrepreneurial spirit in gear and where it will take some time to do so.
Therefore, what about the immediate job crisis we have on our hands? The Minister is taking quite a gamble by leaving everything up to the private sector, and hopefully it will work in the long term, over the next eight or ten years, but there are 1.5 million Canadians who are out of work today and that has to be addressed.
I do not see how those people who were left out of the Budget can be very excited about the investment incentives. In fact, I think they are sorely disappointed. The Budget leaves those Canadians out in the cold. The entrepreneurial spirit proposed in this Budget certainly will achieve some praise from some corners of this country and economy, and I hope it does. But I am telling you, Mr. Speaker, that praise is not going to be very great in Atlantic Canada, especially from those poor people on unemployment insurance whose benefits are running out and who will be unable to get jobs when that happens. These people have to look forward to going on the welfare roles. So this Budget is definitely not about jobs.
I can assure all Hon. Members that this Budget promises to aggravate the economic problems of my province. Prince Edward Island, and the rest of Atlantic Canada. The Budget clearly demonstrates the lack of understanding of Atlantic Canada which this Government suffers from. It is a region hampered by unemployment, where jobs are seasonal, and where the private sector is not the dominant force in the economy. This Budget baffles Atlantic Canada. They are asking me where the jobs will come from and it is obvious that

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Henderson
the Minister does not have the answer, so the Budget is bitter medicine for those people in that part of the country.
The riding I represent, Egmont, is much like other areas of Atlantic Canada. It relies heavily on transfer payments from the federal Government. Those payments are the largest single source of revenue for Prince Edward Island, and now the Minister of Finance has shown to Canadians that job creation is not a priority goal with this Government. The Minister delivered another blow to my province with this holdback of $2 billion in transfer payments over the next five years. Is that fair to the have-not provinces of this country? It means that essential medical services will be curtailed and in some cases eliminated, and dollars for post secondary education will shrink. Atlantic Canadians, especially those in Prince Edward Island, will have to dig pretty deep for this deficit-slashing Budget.
We have heard for the last three months the cliche that the Budget would be tough but fair, so let us look at the fairness of this Budget. First, the average family loses the federal tax reduction of $50. The child tax credit will be lowered. Family allowance cheques will shrink. On top of that, the average family gets hit with taxes on items like pet food, soft drinks, candy and band-aids, all of which are essential to the ordinary and poor Canadian.
Of course, the financial squeeze gets even tougher as we look at other areas where the Government is going to increase taxes, especially the gasoline tax. I happen to live in an area with three main industries: agriculture, the fishery and tourism. For Atlantic Canada as a whole you can add the forestry and mining sectors. These sectors are all heavy users of energy, and when you hit them with that kind of a tax it has to be extremely regressive. Therefore these excessive taxes will pinch the average wage earner, Canadians who scrape from one pay cheque to another. The Minister wants them to spend their savings and they will, but not on investments to stimulate the economy. No, they will cash in their savings to survive, to save their families from poverty. So it is not the families earning $50,000 and more who are going to be hurt. The families who can least afford it, the ones earning $20,000 or $25,000, or even up to $30,000, are going to pay for this Budget.
As I read through the Budget papers, another important concern for Prince Edward Island was totally lacking. There was no mention whatsoever of an energy agreement between the Province of Prince Edward Island and the Government of Canada. The Premier in his 1982 election campaign announced with great fanfare that we were going to have a 20 per cent reduction in energy rates. That was three years ago and what has happened since? There has been not only no reduction, but in fact a 30 per cent increase.
The Prime Minister, during the election campaign, promised to rectify that situation for Prince Edward Island. He recognized, as we all do, that energy rates were too high and he was going to quickly reduce them whenever he got the reins of power. Conservative members were in Halifax during the election campaign and they also said that they were going to find a solution to the energy situation in Prince Edward Island.
The Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. McMillan), who is from Prince Edward Island, said that when they got power we would have a one-shot subsidy. But nothing has happened; in fact it has gone the other way. How long can Prince Edward Islanders continue to shell out to cover their astronomical power bills? It is taking everything they have to turn on the light switch and heat their homes. I can see where the Government is fattening its coffers by proposing a 10 per cent tax on things such as wood stoves, insulation, wind generators and solar panels, all equipment used for alternate energy sources. At the same time we are trying to get these people in the hard-hit regions off high cost non-renewable energy resources and onto renewable energy resources. All the incentive is directed toward western Canada, and particularly the Province of Alberta.
The Maritime provinces are the major producers of potatoes in Canada. Forty-five per cent of Canadian potatoes are harvested in Atlantic Canada. However, Maritime farmers are no longer able to boast about this prize crop because when the statement of the Minister of Finance was introduced in November they were hit with all kinds of fees. On top of that there will be a 2 cent a litre increase on fuel just at the time when farmers are harvesting their crops. That is another sector which is hopelessly going into the hole. The farmers of the country were looking for some relief from interest on loans. Instead another $50 million of farm subsidies was cut from the Budget for next year and every year thereafter, in addition to the cuts which were made in November. It is very difficult for farmers to put up with these uncertainties. They already have to put up with the uncertainties of prices, weather, and escalating energy costs.
Another important group of people living on Prince Edward Island is the senior citizens. Prince Edward Island has the highest per capita rate of senior citizens in Canada. Due to the de-indexing of Old Age Security payments their cheques will not stretch as far next year or in the following years. They will be cut by 3 per cent every year. Many seniors in the country are already living in poverty. Why did the Government take a swipe at the elderly, most of whom are women, who rely solely upon Old Age Security cheques to buy groceries and pay the rent? Three per cent means an awful lot to these people. Three per cent puts food on their tables. Senior citizens will have fewer dollars to spend on consumer goods. That, coupled with the absence of a significant job creation program, will swell the unemployment and welfare rolls. These people merely get by and do not have extra cash to spend. How will that help small businesses, which rely on consumer spending, to create jobs?
A family business which was incorporated 125 years ago went into receivership a week and one-half ago. Approximately 95 to 125 employees will be unemployed. That is the kind of business that we need in Atlantic Canada to create jobs. It is all tied to consumer spending. This Budget has not addressed that situation. In fact, it is going the opposite way. Being faced with even more cuts, it will be very difficult for any company
May 27, 1985

to take over R. T. Holman's and make it work. We desperately need to put Canadians back to work. This Budget is definitely not designed to do that.
Let us consider the fishery. During the election campaign we heard an awful lot about the fishery. We heard of all the things the Government was going to do for fishermen. It almost sounded like Orwell's book of fiction entitled 1984 in which he predicted what society would be like in 1984. The Tories also had a great book of fiction about the fishery. The number one author of that book was the present Prime Minister who had a riding in Atlantic Canada at that time. He was then showing some concern for Atlantic Canada. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) was the co-author of that book.
After the Prime Minister got elected and formed the Government he forgot what Atlantic Canada was all about. The proof of this was in the November 8, 1984 economic statement. In this anti-Robin Hood, take from the poor and give to the rich Budget, the nasty sheriff of Nottingham Forest, the Minister of Finance, robbed one of Canada's poorest industries, the fishing industry, of some $40 million in November. On top of that he has robbed them of $25 million for next year.
Since the Government has taken office we have seen a hefty increase in the staff of the Prime Minister's office. There has been an increase in the staff of Minister's offices. There are 80,000 plus people employed in Ministers' offices. The only reason I can see for this is to find new and better ways to take money from the poor. That is exactly what they have been doing. They have been taking money away from fishermen and farmers. The "new and better" that was talked about during the election campaign was a new way for the poor and middle-class to become poorer and a better way for the rich to become richer.
I feel a bit sorry for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Recently he came to the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry and asked all members of the committee to support him in his attempt to get far more money for small craft harbours. I have proposed on several occasions that we should have no less than $150 million for small craft harbours in Canada. I think every Member of Parliament agrees that there is not enough money in the Budget for small craft harbours. Even Members of Parliament from Ontario and Quebec have come before the committee asking for more money. Last week we had $54 million but on Thursday night we discovered that we have only $25 million left in the global budget of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. This is crazy, Mr. Speaker. It is penny wise and dollar foolish. Our wharves are collapsing before the Government's eyes for need of maintenance. If the maintenance is not done this year it will cost five times as much next year. We have severe ice problems in Altantic Canada and there is a lot of destruction during the winter due to storms. If the necessary repairs are not made we could lose a total wharf. Instead of costing $100,000 to do the repairs now, it will cost the Government $1 million in the future.
The Budget-Mr. Henderson
This is an area in which the Government could look to create jobs. That would provide the infrastructure to expand the fishing and agricultural industries. Unless something is done to provide this infrastructure and keep it in place jobs will be lost. Fishermen can no longer afford to take part in the industry in which they have participated for many years.
I do not know where the Minister will make the cuts in the Budget. He tried in November. It was announced that Ste Anne de Bellevue would be closed and they had to retract that. It was announced that fisheries development programs would be cut in Quebec, Labrador, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. They had to backtrack on that and will have to backtrack on this too.
On behalf of the fishermen of this country whom 1 am trying to represent, I ask the Government to take a more sensible approach to the fishery so that it can become more efficient and create the jobs that are necessary. I hope the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) will heed my words and consider that sector as one which will generate jobs.
The Budget will have a disastrous effect on tourism throughout the country, particularly in my province where it is the third main industry. The majority of tourists from the United States are blue collar workers. They too have budget restrictions, and higher transportation costs will prevent them from staying in Canada longer. That, coupled with the increased ferry rates that were implemented in November, the increased national parks fees as well as other increased costs make it a sad day for Atlantic Canada.
The President of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, Bob Stuart, said in a speech that the impact of the increased investment and expenditure cuts of 10 per cent will mean one per cent growth in central Canada and western Canada and it will mean a minus 6 per cent growth in Atlantic Canada where the private sector makes up just 20 percent of the economy and the public sector accounts for 80 per cent. This is compared to the West where it is 55 per cent in the private sector and 45 per cent for the public sector.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member. I heard him say specifically that farmers in Prince Edward Island are no longer able to boost about their potato crop. I should point out to the House that the Minister of State for Tourism who is the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), the Member for Cardigan (Mr. Binns) and the Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass) consistently boast about the potato crops on Prince Edward Island. The Member represents Prince Edward Island and I think it is shameful that he is not boasting about the potato crops there. 1 hope that his constituents will bring him up short for that.
The Hon. Member has been a member of the Liberal Party and the Liberal Government for several years. He knows that his Party refused to introduce legislation recognizing that the family farm is the pension fund of the farmer. Consistently the

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Henderson
Liberal Party taxed capital gains on the sale of the family farm. The Conservative Party has given the farmers of this country that exemption on capital gains. It is something the Liberal Party refused to do. Is the Hon. Member prepared to agree that this exemption which the Liberals refused to provide will have a long-term effect on the farmers of Canada?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the Hon. Member did not understand what I said. Unfortunately, potato farmers on Prince Edward Island will no longer be able to boast about their potatoes as a result of these increased costs. There will no longer be any potato farmers if the Government proceeds with its increased cost measures. That is what I am saying and that is what his colleagues from Prince Edward Island should be saying.
It is not a question of the quality of our potatoes, it is how long we can continue to grow them at a loss. That is what the Government must consider.
With respect to capital gains, I agree with the positive measure in the Budget. I believe we all agree with that provision and it is a positive move for the farmers who are getting out of agriculture, but is is not positive for those trying to get into agriculture. While a capital gains exemption is an excellent program for farmers, the Government has not addressed the plight of young farmers and new farmers. That is the point I am trying to make to the Government.
Unless it addresses that situation there will be no potatoes in Prince Edward Island to boast about, or any agriculture to boast about. Even milk production is becoming less attractive as a result of high energy costs in Prince Edward Island. The profit margin is almost nothing compared to Ontario. I hope the Government will seriously look at what is happening in Atlantic Canada-particularly my Province of Prince Edward Island-and recognize the situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order for the Hon. Member to be fair about farm issues, he might recall the steps that were taken in November to reduce the input costs and the impact of a 3 per cent or 25 per cent reduction in interest rates on the input costs of farmers and the ability of consumers to pay for the products they produce.
At the beginning of his speech the Hon. Member talked about jobs. He concluded with a special plea for Prince Edward Island because 80 per cent of the economy was in the public sector and 20 per cent was in the private sector. He belongs to a political party that has essentially been in charge of this country for the last 20 years, during which time the proportion of public sector spending has grown in order to keep the community alive, while private sector employment and private sector spending has declined. I found his remarks rather confusing. Does he choose to make that proportion 85 per cent and 15 per cent, 90 per cent and 10 per cent for the future, or does he support our Government's goal of 50-50 in the economy, where everyone has a job because the private sector is strong and healthy? If he believes that, could he identify some measures in that Budget which will help realize that goal?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was quoting a speech given by the President of the Atlantic Provinces Chamber of Commerce. He said that the Budget will decrease by minus 6 per cent the growth of Atlantic Canada. Those were his words, not mine.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is he a Liberal?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know the gentleman. However, after the Budget I presume he would not be a Conservative, if he uses figures like that.
The Hon. Member asked about the ratio in the economy between the public and private sector. I would like to see it at 50-50, just as the Hon. Member would. However, we must be realistic. Cars are not manufactured in the Province of Prince Edward Island, they are manufactured close to the markets. The Hon. Member should know that. We do not have oil wells or spin-off industries from oil wells in the Province of Prince Edward Island. We must rely on three very important industries; agriculture, fisheries and tourism. The other sectors are related to consumer spending.
The disturbing aspect of the budget, as is reflected by the mentality of the Hon. Member, is that Members opposite do not understand what all of Canada is about. They do not understand the situation in Labrador. They do not understand the situation in Cape Breton or they would never have closed two heavy water plants without providing an alternative.
I do not understand downtown Calgary but I suggest it is much easier to create jobs in downtown Calgary, Edmonton, Toronto, Montreal or, indeed, in Ottawa. There are construction cranes everywhere, in Ottawa. I do not think there is one crane in my province of Prince Edward Island. There are some blue herons, but no cranes.
These are areas at which all of us have to take a look. In northern Ontario we will find the same situation. It is not unique to Prince Edward Island or to Cape Breton. There are outlying areas in the country which have to be taken into consideration. Unless the Government is prepared to address the situation, we will have unemployment like we have never seen before. What will happen to the deficit in that event? These people will have to survive. They will have to be paid welfare, UIC or something. All I am saying is that we will have to take a long, hard look at it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member talked about the agricultural industry in Prince Edward Island, and he used some figures regarding fuel prices which I think were somewhat misleading. Perhaps in fairness he might want to correct what he said. He talked about the price going up in September by two cents per litre, but he neglected to mention that on June 1 it would go down .7 cents. Therefore the net additional cost to consumers in September will in fact be 1.3 cents per litre. He gave no credit whatsoever for the fact that the Government, since assuming office, has given a federal tax
May 27, 1985

remission to primary industries, which happens to include farmers as well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on that question and to set the record straight. The tax remission which was given as a result of the November economic statement went into effect on January 1, 1985. It expires, and this is what we have to watch in these Budgets and economic statements-this is the trickery which I am glad to be able to expose today-on January 1, 1987. It is for two seasons. On top of that, they have already put on two cents per litre as well as the other increase last November. Where is the net benefit of that to farmers? There was no mention of that when the Conservative Party promised that if it was elected it would eliminate the excise tax on gasoline for two years. Conservative Members said that they would eliminate it. I have their list of promises. There is no sunset clause on it whatsoever. It was a good idea, a tremendous idea, but many farmers went to the polls to vote thinking that ever after there would be no tax on gasoline. What did the Government do? It will be the same this coming September as it was last August.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A short question by the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I find the comments of the Hon. Member interesting. If one were to believe all that he was saying, one would expect that the netted gems on Prince Edward Island no longer see eye to eye. Bearing in mind that the Hon. Member indicated that the tax on gasoline was going somewhat higher, some 1.3 cents per litre in total, would he not concede, nevertheless, that it will be cheaper than when the Liberals were last in office?
Further, bearing in mind that one of the major costs to agriculture is the cost of capitalization, does the Hon. Member not recognize that interest rates are now 3 per cent cheaper then they were when he was on the government benches about a year ago? He said that we did nothing with the capital gains tax for new farmers to get started and that it would only help older, retiring farmers. Does he not recognize that the removal of $500,000 in capital gains tax will have a downward pressure on land prices and therefore make it more possible for younger farmers to become established?
Does the Hon. Member not huff and puff a bit too hard by not recognizing that part way through our term one of the major aspects at which we are looking is opening up the market to the United States? This could make his netted gems happy again and give farmers an opportunity for some sales. Surely he puffs too hard after being a Member on the Government side.
Finally, does the Hon. Member project a continuation of the Liberal policies of ever increasing the debt, ever increasing the burden, and believing that somehow that creates jobs and economic stability?
