subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured, as a government Member from western Canada, to join in this budget debate. My constituency of Swift Current-Maple Creek covers 18,000 square miles in the southwestern corner of Saskatchewan. The main business and occupation is agriculture, with some secondary oil and gas activity. What I say will be from that perspective.
The Budget is very important to my area of the Prairies, indeed to all western Canada, because it was this area, perhaps more than any other, which endured hardship and neglect over the past 20 years. Western Canada was particularly devastated by twin hammer blows 10 years apart. The 1971 Budget brought us capital gains and 1981 brought us the MacEachen Budget and the infamous National Energy Program. The emancipation of western Canada was launched at the historic meeting in the City of Prince Albert last July. There the Progressive Conservative Party confirmed that western Canada had to be brought back into Confederation. The Prince Albert Declaration indicated that a Progressive Conservative government would prove to western Canadians, by listening and taking action, that the federal Government was as much their Government as that of any other region; westerners would again see Ottawa as a friend, not as a foe.
Last September Canadians voted for change. They voted not just for a change in policies, they voted for a new approach to making public policy. Two months later, in November, we set out our agenda for economic renewal, an agenda which laid out our principles and new policy directions. We said at that

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. G. Wilson
time that we would make the changes necessary to promote growth, create jobs and improve social programs. We said that we would act fairly, and we said that we would consult and listen before acting.
Since that time we have listened to the concerns and aspirations of Canadians in the most extensive consultative process in Canadian history. However, consultation has not been an excuse for inaction. Since September we have implemented many of the policies defined in Prince Albert. We said that we would implement a taxation system which recognized bottom line profits as the basis for assessing taxes in order to stimulate the investment needed to bring on new energy resources. In keeping with this, the Western Accord has been signed, thus concluding negotiations with the western provinces and the oil industry. The Western Accord signals a new era in federal-provincial relations and the end of the national energy policy. This new policy will mean opportunity for all Canadians through balanced development of our resources for all regions. Jobs in exploration and drilling will mean jobs in manufacturing plants. Development in the oil and gas resource areas will mean jobs and growth in Ontario and Quebec. The Western Accord brings to a close that bitter chapter of western history in which the federal Government unilaterally changed the rules of the game and caused untold misery for hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
In the areas of transportation and agriculture we have frozen existing freight rates from further increases for the next two crop years. The 31.5 tonne volume cap in the Western Grain Transportation Act is being removed. We have preserved a number of rural rail branch lines. We have implemented the $60 million federal-provincial drought assistance program. The Farm Credit Corporation has reduced interest rates by some 4 per cent for 5,600 farmers. It has announced a shared risk mortgage program. We have allowed voluntary dual labelling in imperial as well as in metric on farm products.
Last fall this Government reduced the price of fuel to primary producers by some 22 cents a gallon. We are in the process of legislating a national voluntary tripartite red meat stabilization program. We amended the Western Grain Stabilization Act to trigger a timely and substantial pay-out of $450 million to producers. The strong-arm and confrontational tactics of the Department of National Revenue have been abolished and taxpayers' rights have been enshrined in the declaration. All these actions prove this Government's commitment to the needs of western Canadians and to Canadian farmers.
On Thursday last, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) reaffirmed this commitment when he announced the immediate $500,000 capital gains exemption on the sale of farm property while at the same time preserving the tax free intergenerational rollover of land. Since the Liberal Government instituted capital gains in 1972, that unfair tax has hung like a poisonous cloud over the farm community. It hit hardest the
farmer who found the fruits of his life's work locked up in the ground and, on retirement, subject to considerable income tax.
I am privileged to be a member of the Standing Committee on Finance of this House, a committee which in the month of March held extensive hearings on a number of agricultural issues and listened to briefs and presentations from all sectors of agriculture. From these hearings, it became obvious that the major concern was capital gains. The elimination of capital gains on farmland will enable a generation of older farmers to turn over their farm and receive a fair price which will permit them to retire with some dignity. At the same time, opportunities will open up to younger farmers to acquire this land at a more reasonable price. A further benefit will accrue to agriculture through obvious simplification in farm estate planning. In most instances, the lifetime capital gains exemption will do away with the widespread use of phoney custom work contracts and other back-door agreements which maintain roll over eligibility. Western agriculture today rejoices in the elimination of this odious and unfair impediment to individual freedom. The spirit and intent of the Prince Albert declaration manifests itself once again.
Thus far I have concentrated on our actions to help Canadian farmers, but farmers have wider interests. I know they share our concerns for the future of this country, for the unemployed and for our national financial problems, so I want to leave the subject of agriculture and talk generally about the comprehensive plan for economic review and renewal which the Minister of Finance unveiled on budget afternoon.
I, along with many other new Members, entered this federal level of public life because we feared for the future, the future of our families, our children and for their children, indeed for the very future of our way of life. We could see we were heading in the wrong direction. We were at the crossroads, the crisis stage, as the interest on the debt begins to feed on itself like a snowball rolling downhill. This Budget represents an historic moment in Canadian history. It is a watershed. It represents the turning point, the beginning of the ascension from the far depths of the fiscal imprudence of the past administration.
There is no magic to it. It faces the fundamental truth. You cannot spend indefinitely that which you do not have. There will be no more bribing Canadians with their own money, no more spend now and pay later. This Budget is realistic, fair, effective and honest. It is based on extensive consultation with Canadians.
This Budget is part of the agenda announced November last, an agenda for action to break the vicious circle of high unemployment and spiralling national debt. This Government seeks to break that cycle by taking decisive action on three fronts: first, by encouraging private initiative enterprise and productive investment by increasing the availability of capital and by rewarding success instead of merely subsidizing effort; second, by managing Government more effectively; and third, by gaining control of the national debt through a realistic medium-term strategy.

May 27, 1985
This Budget represents a fundamental break with the past, a significant change of direction as Canadians turn away from big Government toward the private sector, particularly small business, for growth and jobs. The personal lifetime capital gains exemption is designed to let all people of Canada- individual Canadians who have a personal stake in their affairs-to choose when and where to invest and how to create jobs. For too long politicians and bureaucrats, who have no investment, have been telling Canadians what to do. It has not worked, and it never will. There is no substitute for individual decision-making by Canadians who can best decide for themselves their own course of action. The jobs will follow. This is no great leap of faith; it is just plain common sense.
Government has become too big. It has become part of the problem instead of being part of the solution. That is why we have been combing Government for waste and inefficiency since September, and our efforts are starting to pay off. We will be lowering government overhead, rationalizing and improving government programs and selling off Crown corporations which do not serve an essential public policy purpose. The civil service will be reduced and public sector pensions put on a sounder footing. The search is still on to ensure that we provide maximum value for tax dollars.
This Government is first putting its own House in Order. It will be leaner, more efficient and cost effective, but savings from this better management will not be enough in itself to end the debt spiral. In order to deal with this problem we must increase growth, reduce spending and increase taxes, because failure to contain the debt now will force future Governments to drastic measures. We must reduce spending now to save programs later.
It is important that Canadians understand the magnitude of our deficit and debt problem and why it poses serious risks to our ability to achieve sustained economic growth and full employment. The public debt is simply the sum of all past deficits. It took 100 years to accumulate a debt of $18 billion and now, less than two decades later, the debt is approaching $200 billion, and is doubling every five years. Like any borrower, the Canadian Government pays interest on the debt and, like any borrower, the Government has been affected by high interest rates. Interest charges have been the fastest growing component of government expenditure. However, unlike most individual Canadians, the Government has been borrowing additional funds to pay the interest on past debts. That is why our debt is spiralling out of sight. If we do not show the resolve to deal with this problem now, the inevitable result will be the financial paralysis of the Government of Canada.
This Government has inherited a fiscal mess of such magnitude that urgent remedial action must be taken. Government spending has virtually doubled in the past four years. Expenditures today exceed revenues by 50 per cent. Government spends more on your behalf, 50 per cent more in fact than it gathers in taxes and other revenues. The deficit is growing three times faster than the economy. This year's deficit is approximately $35 billion. For every three dollars spent, two
The Budget-Mr. G. Wilson
are collected and one is borrowed. Surely even the most profligate spendthrift would agree that this cannot long continue. We are mortgaging our tomorrow, our children's future to pay for today's excesses.
The annual deficit or shortfall amounts to about $1,400 per Canadian or approximately $5,600 for a family of four. Any family that continues to spend $5,600 more each year than it takes in will soon find itself in financial jeopardy. That family may be able to borrow for a while, but the interest charges will mount up and it will soon be faced with hard choices: to bring in more money, to spend less or declare bankruptcy, and the option of bankruptcy is not open to Government.
The net national debt is now closing in on $200 billion. It is not the debt itself that is the problem. It is the cost of the debt, the interest burden. This is not a little interest free loan from mom and dad. This is a cross that all Canadians have to bear. This year alone, $25 billion will be required to pay interest on the previously accumulated debt, the Liberal legacy. This is about $1,000 per person this year alone. One out of every $4 the Government spends goes to interest. One out of every three dollars of government revenue goes to service the debt. Projecting this kind of fiscal insanity into the future will indicate that all revenues may be required to service the debt in the 1990s.
What then? We might try to borrow money, but that just continues to build up future problems. At some point the bills come due. We could simply print more money, but to do that would guarantee an outbreak of inflation and rising interest rates that would damage confidence, investment and growth in the same way it did in the 1970s and early 1980s. This would be an abdication of responsibility. It is not an option.
The only other choice would be to find the money through drastic cuts in government services and major tax increases. Many government programs would be in jeopardy. Obviously this is also unacceptable. This situation is so compelling that I am sure all Members of this House will understand that the matter of reduced government spending, consequent debt reduction and lower interest rates are conditions precedent for greater employment and job opportunity for Canadians. I know that Members will unite and support these budget proposals which are necessary, and at the same time fair and reasonable. The people of Canada expect their representatives to put the fiscal house in order. They expect a responsible and prudent response. They want deficit reduction. They want to get this country moving again.
Some say that faster economic growth will solve our fiscal dilemma. As the Minister of Finance said, it will be an important part of the solution and the measures we have introduced will boost economic growth, but growth alone will not solve our problem. If we are to get off this treadmill, we must also slow down the debt spiral through lower deficits and lower interest rates, and that is what we have done in this Budget. We have taken that decisive first step to arrest and reverse the trend of increasing annual deficits. We have taken the tough decisions necessary to prevent future disaster. Though the measures are tough, they are also fair. Most

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. G. Wilson
important, they are being implemented in a way that will not threaten our economic recovery. The Government has consciously chosen a plan of action which controls the deficit now while ensuring substantial reductions in the future. It is a plan that will help us create jobs now and ensure that we can create even more jobs later.
Many Hon. Members have heard or read that the Government is obsessed with the deficit. That is simply not true. Our obsession is with jobs; good, satisfying and lasting jobs for Canadians. If we believed higher deficits and a rapidly growing debt, the Liberal legacy, would help us create those jobs, we would gladly have increased the deficit. In the past four years, the deficit has tripled and unemployment has doubled. Obviously that approach does not work. It has not in the past and it never will.
Government job creation is band-aid stuff: twenty weeks of work and then back onto unemployment insurance. That is not good enough. Instead, the Government has brought in a realistic agenda for action that tackles our problems as they exist and as we found them on taking office last September. When we set out the problems and our directions for solving them in November, we were not building illusions. We were honest with Canadians. We accepted our mandate for change and made clear that implementing and adjusting to change would test the strength and resolve of all of us. We promised to act but first we promised to consult fully and openly with Canadians in reaching the decisions presented in the Budget.
We have acted to control and reduce deficits in a balanced and careful way that will not tip the economy off its current course of action. However, we acted with firmness and determination because, without control of our accumulating debt, the economy would be unable to produce the jobs we need.
This Budget is responsible, effective and fair. It is responsible because it faces up to the challenges, the same challenges that were irresponsibly ignored by the former Government. It is effective because, it reduces the deficit by $4 billion this year and by $8 billion next year and reduces growth in the national debt. It is fair because the measures to reduce the deficit do not endanger the economic recovery. All Canadians are asked to contribute fairly and equitably, but those in greatest need receive adequate protection.
The Minister of Finance should be congratulated for carefully constructing a package that must be viewed in its entirety. We must go past the individual trees to look at the forest. The Budget asks individuals and corporations to pay their fair shares, and it also uses the tax system to promote economic growth and job creation. It contains expenditure reductions and program reviews and it also increases funding for job-creation and training programs and raises the child tax credit for lower-income Canadians.
This is a Budget for the 1980s. It builds on our strengths for a better Canada and a better tomorrow. It indicates to individual Canadians that for too long Government has made their decisions for them. Now is the time to revitalize, to
rejuvenate and to transform ideas and energies into the kind of Canada we all want for ourselves and our children.
The Budget is realistic. It is fair and it will be effective. It will be effective because the action we have taken in this Budget reflects our faith in people, our faith in the ingenuity and drive of individual Canadians to seize opportunities and invest in their own futures.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for a very excellent speech which was splendidly delivered. I was interested in what he had to say about capital gains. Member mentioned very carefully that capital gains formed the nest-egg of farmers and businessmen, and that is quite right. In fact, it is the only nest-egg they have. However, it goes beyond that.
One day I was standing on the street in Black Diamond when a businessman of about 35 or 40 years of age came up to me. He asked me, "When are you going to remove this capital gains tax?" I asked him why he was interested in that as he was not ready to retire. He said he was not ready to retire but he went on to say, "See that land there beside my service station? I own that. I would like to expand that business by hiring another seven people, but as long as the capital gains tax exists, which will rob me of my heritage, I will not do it. I will work my fingers to the bone for my wife and my children but I will not do it for any blankety-blank government".
I wonder how many businessmen have refused to expand their businesses because of capital gains taxes. This measure is not just for the rich, is is for everyone.
There is another point I would like to mention but I do not have the time as I know that these questions are to be short and concise. The Hon. Is he aware of the terrible attitude of western members of the NDP who say that capital gains tax elimination is only for the rich? I wonder if the Hon. Without doubt, capital gains tax has hung like a sword over their heads since its inception. It has backed up a whole generation of older farmers and business-people who have been basically unable to dispose of their assets to the next generation because of the prospect of that unfair tax
May 27, 1985

hanging over their heads. This measure will stimulate activity all across Canada, and, more important, I think it gives the younger generation an opportunity to strive and to succeed.
I know, as do many of my confreres, of many young people who are bushy-tailed and eager to get out to work. They want to work long hours. It is my understanding, that effective June 1, as a result of the Western Accord, oil prices will be deregulated. At that time the Canadian Ownership Special Charge will be abolished. Members will recall that the COSC was imposed in 1981 as part of the original National Energy Program. Its
The Budget-Mr. G. Wilson
purpose was to allow Petro-Canada to embark on expansion plans. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering the debate on the Budget, I have cause to reflect once again on what the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops stated in their report which was released January 5, 1983. The report was entitled, "Ethical Reflections on the Economic Crisis". At that time, the Bishops gave a general description of the realities which faced Canadians. They said:
Along with most people in Canada today, we realize that our economy is in serious trouble. In our own regions, we have seen the economic realities of plant shut-downs, massive layoffs of workers, wage restraint programs, and suspension of collective bargaining rights for public sector workers. At the same time, we have seen the social realities of abandoned one-industry towns, depleting unemployment insurance benefits, cut-backs in health and social services, and line-ups at local soup kitchens. And, we have also witnessed, first-hand, the results of a troubled economy: personal tragedies, emotional strain, loss of human dignity, family breakdown, and even suicide.
In reading that statement, and looking at the Budget which was brought down by the Conservative Party, I am concerned about the way in which the Budget addresses the realities which the Bishops laid out in their statement of 1983. 1 found a lot of what the Bishops spoke about in 1983, and the criticisms which they had of the Liberal Government and its economic policies, are very much applicable to the Budget which was delivered last Thursday.
For example, in the statement, the Bishops pointed out that the economic strategy of the Liberal Government was one which they described as:
To stimulate economic growth, Governments are being called upon to provide a more favourable climate for private investments. Since capital tends to flow wherever the returns are greatest, reduced labour costs and lower taxes are required if countries are to remain competitive. As a result, most Governments are introducing austerity measures such as wage restraint programs, cut-backs in social services and other reductions in social spending in order to attract more private investment.
Again, what the Bishops pointed out in their 1983 statement is very much what this Government and previous Liberal Governments have done. They have reduced taxes in order to encourage private investment at the expense of social programs, in the hope that it would generate the economic activity which would benefit the majority of Canadians.
The Bishops' statement continued:
As recent economic policy statements reveal, the primary objective is to restore profitability and competitiveness in certain Canadian industries and provide more favourable conditions for private investment in the country. They private sector is to be the "engine" for economic recovery.
It is that economic order about which the Bishops wrote. Their statement continued:
-we firmly believe that present economic realities reveal a "moral disorder" in our society.
The Budget which was brought down by the Conservative Government is a moral disorder. It is a budget based on false premises, based on the notion of greed and encouraging the accumulation of private and corporate wealth in obscene proportions.
Let us have a look, Mr. Speaker, at past records to see whether this economic policy of encouraging the private sector in order to have economic renewal has actually worked. Let us look first at some of the corporate tax breaks which exist now.
For example, in 1983, Northern Telecom, had $3.3 billions in sales, showed $325 million in profit, yet managed to end the fiscal year paying no taxes. TransCanada PipeLines Limited has $4.7 billion in assets and its 1982 pre-tax earnings were $482 million, yet it paid just 7 per cent in taxes. Shell Canada Limited, with assets of $4.7 billion and pre-tax earnings of $302 million, paid no income tax in 1982.
This Government talks about fairness. Is it fair that Shell Canada and Imperial Oil pay no taxes when they make hundreds of millions of dollars? But the poor person who is earning $15,000 to $20,000 a year will have removed out of his pocket $1,000 because of this Tory Government. Is that fair? Is that equitable? I agree with the bishops when they say there is a moral disorder in this country and in this economy.
There is the other area of tax deferrals, Mr. Speaker. In 1982 it was estimated that we had some $29 billion owing, increasing by approximately $1 billion every year. So let us assume that in 1985 we have $32 billion or $33 billion in tax deferrals. These are taxes which corporations admit they owe, but they made an agreement with the Government that the taxes would be deferred until some time in the future. Will they ever be paid? No, Mr. Speaker. Anyone who is wise in the ways of the world knows that these taxes will never be paid. Is any interest charged on these taxes? No, Mr. Speaker, none whatsoever.
The Government, of course, has to pay interest on money it borrows. I heard the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson) explain that anyone who borrows money has to pay interest so, therefore, the Government has to pay interest on its deficits. Yet there is some $30 billion out there owed to the federal Government. Is any interest being paid on that money? No, Mr. Speaker. If the Government would only charge interest at 10 per cent on the $30 billion, it would collect $3 billion this year which would reduce the deficit to a much greater extent than did the Minister of Finance last Thursday evening. Thel Governmenticould just collect 10 per
May 27, 1985

cent interest on the $30 billion which is owing to it. That is a very handy and neat way of reducing the deficit. Charging 10 per cent interest is just one little item. Most people who borrow money in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, would love to pay 10 per cent interest on their borrowings. Many small business people and many farmers would love to pay 10 per cent interest. That's fair, isn't it? Let's charge 10 per cent interest on these deferred taxes. We can really reduce the deficit with some $3 billion. But, no, Mr. Speaker, the Gover-nemnt is not going to touch those corporations.
There is also the research and development tax credit, Mr. Speaker, which is something that our Liberal friends introduced. We were going to lose some $200 million on this. But apparently, we have lost some $2.8 billion on the R and D tax credits. Are we going to put a stop to this? No, Mr. Speaker. When the Tories came in they realized it was a little too much so they introduced a grandfather clause. When the Tories took power it was estimated we had lost some $1.5 billion in lost government revenues just on this one scam alone-and it is a scam. The Minister of Finance knows it's a scam. Every Hon. Member opposite knows it's a scam. There is no $2.8 billion in new research and development which has occurred in this country. So the Conservatives were going to shut that down. At that stage it was estimated we had lost some $1.5 billion. Some shut down, Mr. Speaker. We lost another $1.3 billion under the research and development tax credit scam after the Tories were in. And they say, "No problem. Let's feed those guys some more tax breaks and eventually some of it will trickle down and create some jobs. Prosperity is just around the corner".
But, Mr. Speaker, as the bishops pointed out in their statement, "Since capital tends to flow to wherever the returns are greater, reduced labour cost and lower taxes are required if countries are to remain competitive".
What we are doing is giving these corporations more tax incentives and tax breaks in order to compete with what is given by the Governments of the United States, England and in other places. So it continues, Mr. Speaker, and the result is that the wealthy and the multinationals, who have the power to move their capital around the globe, essentially hold this Government, and Governments around the world, up for ransom. That results in the wealthy and the multinationals not paying their fair share. All this budget has done is give further service to the corporate sector.
Let us continue to look at the Tory philosophy of helping the well to do. I have a copy of The Globe and Mail of July 7, 1984. The headline reads, "Unemployment Good Alberta Minister Says", and I quote:
Unemployment is good for the economy because it controls wage levels and increases productivity. Alberta manpower Minister Ernest Isley says.
"From an economic point of view, if you define full employment as everyone having a job, that's not a healthy thing"-
The Minister says full employment is not a healthy thing. I am waiting for some of the Tories to come out of the closet and repeat what the Alberta Minister of Manpower says, because I believe that a fair number of those Tories do not
The Budget-Mr. de Jong
really believe in full employment. They believe in keeping working people down and reducing the cost of manufacturing so that we can compete with the wage levels of Hong Kong and Singapore. That is what those Hon. Members want. They do not believe in full employment because what full employment will do is allow working people to get better wages and they are not interested in that. All they are interested in is having the corporate sector, their wealthy friends, doing quite all right, thank you.
Then there are some 7,782 persons who paid no tax this year. These are people who earn more than $50,000 or $60,000 a year and pay absolutely no tax because of all of the different loopholes and schemes in which they can get involved. The Government says, "We are going to get these characters. We are introducing this surtax". But that is a joke, Mr. Speaker. The surtax is a tax on the tax that you pay. But the 7,782 people who earn more than $60,000 who didn't pay any tax, are not going to be paying a surtax. All the surtax will do is penalize those people who do not play the tax loophole game. It is going to force those people who have been paying their fair share of the tax, and who have not gotten involved in any of the tax avoidance schemes, to get involved in tax avoidance schemes. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the surtax will produce less revenue than is now being collected because it will encourage people to attempt to avoid taxes through different tax schemes.
We come now to the other goody in the Budget, the capital gains goody. The Tories are quite smart. They have learned some lessons from the Liberals and definitely from the Republicans in the U.S. Essentially what they have done is taken one good item and used that as an excuse to bring in all sorts of questionable items. They allowed farmers to escape paying taxes on $500,000 of capital gains. This is a good move. It is something which has been in our-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could you please ask the jackasses to stop braying.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not a nice thing to say about the NDP.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is something which has been-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. There will be an opportunity to ask questions or make comments after the Hon. Member's speech.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that item has been in the NDP platform for most of the 1970s. However, the problem is that the Government at the same time is allowing tax-free capital gains for all sorts of wheelers and dealers and speculators. To achieve one good thing they have drafted legislation which is so broad I predict it will put to shame the Liberal research and development tax credit scheme so far as Government revenue loss is concerned.

May 27, 1985
The Budget-Mr. de Jong
There is a very good reason why a farmer who toils on his land has seen very little return on his labour, especially over the last decade. The reason is that the cost of production is about equal to the prive he gets for the goods he produces. The only profit he really produces is in the improvements to his farm. So when he sells his farm I think it is right and just that he not be taxed on the first $500,000 of his capital gain. But is this also true for people who buy condominiums and flip them a year later? Is it also true for people who speculate? I say it is not.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why not?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because the farmer is engaged in some honest labour, whereas the bloody speculator flipping apartments or condominiums in Florida should be taxed on his capital gain.
So we see a Budget based essentially on a very simple notion of making the guys at the top happy and eventually the benefits will trickle down. It is called the trickle-down theory. Essentially it means feed the horse a lot of oats and eventually the sparrows will get some. That is the essential notion. Except that some Members opposite obviously continue to step in that under the mistaken belief that they are receiving a benefit.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Check the floor by your desk.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We call it the NDP platform.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I claim this Budget is essentially obscene. The Bishops, in their statement, pointed out:
At the same time, working people, the unemployed, young people, and those on fixed incomes are increasingly called upon to make the most sacrifice for economic recovery.
-even if companies recover and increase their profit margins, the additional revenues are likely to be reinvested in more labour-saving technology, exported to other countries, or spent on market speculation or luxury goods.
In this Budget we see that older retired people have been asked to carry the burden; they will be losing $1.6 billion in the next few years. They are the ones who are called-upon to sacrifice in order to reduce the deficit. Yet there is no call for Imperial Oil or TransCanada Pipelines or Northern Telecom to pay their share, or for the Government to call in the $30 billion in deferred taxes. No, those companies are not to participate in reducing the deficit, just the old folks, and that I call obscene. It is an obscene Budget and it is certainly not in keeping with the traditions and sentiments of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I listened to the Hon. Member's speech with a great deal of concern. We have expanded the capital gains tax exemption beyond farmers alone, but the previous Liberal Government, as everyone in this House knows, applied that capital gains tax to farmers without any understanding of the situation. No one in this House would doubt the effort made by people who earn their living from the soil, but I am shocked to hear to Hon. Member infer that the tourist operators, hardware store operators, contractors and real estate agents in my riding, all of them
people who make legitimate capital gains by working at what they do best, just as hard as farmers work at what they do best, do not perform honest labour. I ask him to immediately stand in his place and refute the irresponsible charge that those people who work so hard in this country do not achieve what they do through honest labour.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it amazes me how hyped-up Government Members are. Obviously they have gone through a good mind training session. They remind me of a group of Amway salesmen. They have been hyped-up, given the line, and they are out there like little robots delivering their lines and points. Here in the House they are hyped-up to the point of impoliteness and discourtesy, I might add. They have to do this little number of show and tell for Canadians because they realize that this Budget is dishonest, and they have to shout loud and long in order to try and convince the Canadian people they have something worthwhile. But in fact it is the biggest con we have seen in a number of years.
The Hon. Member talks about the hard-working Canadian people that this Budget is supposed to help. I have no doubt that this capital gains provision will help some people who have needed and need help.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Fine. But I want the Hon. Member to stand up and state in this House that it will also help people who do not need to be helped and should not be helped. I challenge the Hon. Member to make that statement right now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I note the Hon. Member is not standing up.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to the Bishops, and I was just going to call a Bishop because I think he is bordering on cardiac arrest. He talked about the Budget being a moral disorder. On the contrary, I think it is a serious act of fiscal responsibility. I think the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) will agree that the Budget is a break from the past. We know the old ways were not working. Pouring funds into the public trough was not creating jobs in the country. The ball is now in the court of all Canadians. It is up to Canadian businesses to invest and create real jobs rather than short-term, make-work projects.
Does the Member for Regina East think the Government should have printed more money which would create inflation? Does he think the Government should continue to pour money down the deficit drain, or does he think we should eliminate short-term, make-work projects in favour of long-term, real, lasting jobs, allowing the private sector to create more jobs in the country?
May 27, 1985

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a very interesting question, Mr. Speaker. As I answer it I wish to note that the former Member to whom I made the challenge chose not to respond to it.
Government studies show that the people who have received the most tax breaks have been the least productive in creating new jobs. I find it amazing that the Tories can say that the Budget is a major break from the past. That is not true. The Lalonde Budget and the MacEachen Budget before it were essentially based on the trickle down notion. The $30 billion in deferred taxes and the drop in the corporate tax rate which has occurred in the last number of years are just continuations of that policy. We must ask whether that policy has worked. It has not.
Will the tax breaks to corporations produce jobs? A Statistics Canada report found that incentives to business are not likely to create more jobs. In the last quarter of 1984 there was "little incentive for most companies to increase their spending on plant and equipment since most sectors are burdened with ... excess capacity". For the manufacturing sector the capacity utilization rate was only 77 per cent. If you are only utilizing 77 per cent of your plant are you going to create more jobs and open more plants? Of course not. Therefore, why does the Hon. Member ask such a silly question? Is it economic sense that if you give someone who is only operating his plant at 77 per cent capacity more tax breaks he will use those tax breaks to build new plants and equipment? Of course he will not. The problem is that the public does not have the income to buy the goods and services which are produced.
I do not understand why the Tories do not understand simple straight economics. It is the lack of people being able to buy the goods and services that they need. We have people lining up at food banks because they do not have the income to go to a grocery store and buy a pound of hamburger. That is why we have a downturn in the economy. No matter how much money is given to the person who is only operating at 77 per cent capacity, he will not increase his capacity. He will only take the money and build condominiums in Florida or use it for a take-over. He will not create jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) when he asks when the Opposition is going to stop running around with a little black cloud over its head.

And I think that if this black cloud is as thick as their arguments are sound it will not cast much of a shadow. A moment ago, I heard the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) say that 7,700 people would not pay any tax, so they would not pay any surtax either.
I would also like to hear the real figures. I draw the attention of the House to the fact that indeed 1.2 million people will pay the surtax in Canada. Well, no one can claim that 1.2 million is a negligible amount compared with the 7,700 people who will not pay any tax.
The Budget-Mr. de Jong
Another interesting figure has to do with the fact that 6,600 companies will also be paying the surtax. Again if we compare that with the 7,700 people mentioned earlier, I think it is a very sad performance.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will give you 30 seconds to respond.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, those are estimates which his Department has produced. I suggest that the surtax will be like a disincentive or penalty for those people who have been paying their tax. They will find themselves paying more tax on the taxes that they have been paying. They will look for tax loopholes and tax avoidance schemes in order to stop paying that tax. I suggest that the surtax may very well mean an over-all drop in revenues because it is a penalty for the people who have been doing the honest thing and paying their taxes.

It being 5.45 o'clock p.m., it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 64(6), to interrupt the proceedings and put forthwith any question necessary to dispose of the amendment to the amendent which is now before the House.
Mr. Wilson, seconded by Mr. Mulroney, has moved:
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the Government.
In amendment thereto, Mr. Johnston, seconded by Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra), has moved:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"this House condemns the Government for its betrayal of the trust of the Canadian people by producing a budget that destroys jobs, that offers neither help nor hope to the working poor and the unemployed, that brutalizes the middle class, that imposes massive and unfair tax increases on middle and lower income Canadians and that is devastating to the economically disadvantaged regions of the country."
In amendment to the amendment, Mr. Riis, seconded by Mr. Murphy, has moved:
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House further condemns the Government for actions which will effectively reduce pensions for senior citizens, for gasoline tax increases to pay for the Western Accord, for its failure to take immediate and determined action to reduce the ranks of the unemployed, and for the absence of a minimum tax on wealthy Canadians who pay no income tax."
The question is on the amendment to the amendment. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the amendment?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.
